## Summary

Mayarin enters **ETHOnline 2026** (4–16 September) with one build across six sponsors: **Mayarin Agent Rail** — an x402 payment rail that makes any Mayarin-gated endpoint payable by an AI agent that has never seen an API key, a signup form, or a docs page.

Six sponsors, one flow, seven RFCs:

| RFC | Sponsor | Role in the flow | Pool |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #207 | — | The spine: x402 v2 over the clearing engine | — |
| #208 | Arc (Circle) | USDC-native settlement rail; agent wallets on the payer side | \$10,000 |
| #209 | Hedera | Second rail; the live gated service, via Blocky402 | \$6,000 |
| #210 | Privy | Merchant organization wallet; the payer-side signing port | \$5,000 |
| #211 | Uniswap Foundation | Exact-output swap so the merchant is paid exactly | \$5,000 |
| #212 | Bazantic | Discovery — how an agent finds the rail at all | \$3,000 |
| #213 | Chainlink | The reference price that can refuse an execution | \$500 |

Nothing here is a wrapper written for a prize. Each sponsor occupies a position the rail needs filled: a chain, a wallet, a swap direction, a price guard, a discovery surface.

## Motivation

Mayarin's current integration story is: a merchant reads the docs, takes an API key, writes code. That works and it is not going away.

The rail adds a second story with no human in it. An agent requests a resource, gets `402 Payment Required` with machine-readable terms, signs an authorization for exactly the stated amount, retries, and receives the resource. The merchant is priced in their own currency and settled in a stablecoin, exactly as they are today. The agent never registered.

Everything x402 requires, Mayarin already runs — quote lock, idempotent and resumable state machine, double-entry ledger, treasury broadcast. What is missing is the wire format and one execution path. That asymmetry is why six sponsor integrations fit in thirteen days: they are adapters on an engine that already works, not an engine.

## The decision that comes before any code

**Continuity or Start Fresh.** Mayarin is a pre-existing project, so the default is the continuity tracks — and that default is expensive:

| Sponsor | Continuity only | Start Fresh |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arc | \$3,166 | \$6,834 |
| Hedera | \$1,000 | \$6,000 |
| Uniswap | \$2,000 | \$3,000 |

The alternative: the Agent Rail ships as a **new repository** that consumes `@mayarin/*` as a dependency. It is genuinely a new product built on top of Mayarin rather than an extension of it, which is what the Start Fresh tracks describe. Whether each sponsor reads it that way is theirs to say.

**Decided 3 September: Continuity.** Mayarin enters as itself, extending the existing repository, and the lower figures above are the working exposure. Still confirm in each sponsor's Discord that a continuity submission is registered the way that sponsor expects — Arc states it outright ("must be registered as a Continuity Project"), and a submission filed against the wrong track is a disqualification discovered at judging rather than a lost point.

## Goals

- One coherent demo in which all six sponsors are load-bearing, not decorative.
- Six submissions, six videos, each argued from that sponsor's angle.
- Every piece lands in the architecture the repository already has: ports in `core`, adapters in `providers`, wiring in `apps/api/src/container.ts`.
- Nothing merged that would embarrass the codebase on 17 September.

## Non-Goals

- Winning every track. Arc and Hedera are the two worth losing sleep over.
- Shipping any of this to mainnet during the event.
- Deployments of record. Every new-chain and new-contract deployment in this batch is a throwaway v0 whose address does not reach the SDK, the docs, or a demo link.
- Fiat rails and the off-ramp. Still out of the MVP, still out of this.

## Specification

### Sequence

**4–5 September — foundation.**
Track registration confirmed with all six sponsors. `feat/arbitrum-chain-support` merged to `main` — it car
title: RFC: ETHOnline 2026 — Mayarin Agent Rail, six sponsors on one x402 flow

## Bug Description / Feature Request

The AI Agent node (`@n8n/n8n-nodes-langchain.agent`) re-establishes the MCP connection and re-fetches `tools/list` from **every attached MCP Client Tool sub-node before every model call** within a single execution. With multiple MCP tool sub-nodes attached, this adds a large, fixed dead-time cost to **every agent iteration**, dominating wall-clock time for multi-turn agent runs.

We measured this with a controlled dose-response experiment (details below): **each attached MCP Client Tool sub-node costs ≈7.0 seconds per model call**, independent of the size of the server's tool list. At 10 attached MCP sub-nodes, an agent spends ≈60s of dead time before every single model call — a 20-turn agent run pays ~20 minutes of pure reconnect/listTools overhead.

## Measurements (n8n 2.36.8, self-hosted)

Four byte-identical clones of a production agent workflow, differing only in the number of attached MCP Client Tool sub-nodes (all `httpStreamable`, OAuth2, pointing at healthy HTTP MCP servers). Identical synthetic 5-model-call task, 8 interleaved runs per variant (32 runs, 128 inter-call gap samples). Per-turn dead gap = time between consecutive model calls minus tool execution time within the window:

| MCP tool sub-nodes attached | median inter-call dead gap (s/turn) | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.10 | 0.09–0.11 |
| 2 | 12.26 | 10.3–18.4 |
| 5 | 32.04 | 23.9–39.0 |
| 10 | 60.29 | 40.5–97.4 |

**Linear fit: `gap_s = 6.96 × n_tools + 0.26` (R² = 0.67 over all 128 samples).** Model latency stayed flat (~1.4s) across variants — the cost is entirely in the per-iteration MCP connect + `tools/list` round trips. The marginal per-node cost was uniform across small (3-tool) and large (~70-tool) servers — it's connection/handshake overhead, not schema byte size.

The 0-node floor of 0.10s/turn shows the agent loop itself is essentially free; the entire dead time is attributable to per-iteration MCP session re-establishment.

We confirmed the mechanism by consolidating the 10 MCP sub-nodes into 1 (an aggregating MCP endpoint exposing the same tools): median per-turn dead gap dropped from ~46–60s to **~3.4–5.9s** on the same workflow — matching the fit's prediction for n=1.

## Suggested improvement

Cache the MCP client connection and `tools/list` result **per execution** (or with a short TTL), instead of reconnecting and re-listing before every model call in the agent loop. Tool schemas essentially never change mid-execution; a per-execution cache would eliminate this term entirely for every n8n AI Agent user with MCP tools attached. An opt-out (or `listChanged` notification support) could cover servers with genuinely dynamic tool lists.

## To Reproduce

1. Create an AI Agent workflow with a chat/LLM model and attach N MCP Client Tool sub-nodes (HTTP streamable transport) pointing at any healthy MCP servers.
2. Give the agent a scripted task requiring ~5 sequential tool calls (one per turn).
3. Inspect the execution timeline: measure the wall-clock gap between consecutive model calls and subtract tool execution time.
4. Repeat with different N. The dead gap scales linearly with N (~7s per attached MCP sub-node per model call in our environment).

## Expected behavior

Per-iteration overhead should be independent of the number of attached MCP tool sub-nodes (connect + listTools paid once per execution, not once per model call).

## Environment

- n8n version: 2.36.8 (self-hosted, queue mode)
- MCP transport: HTTP streamable, OAuth2 client credentials
- Model node: Anthropic Chat Model
- Related: #33792 (per-sub-node error isolation in `supplyData()` — same code path; a per-execution connection cache would also narrow that failure window)
title: AI Agent re-connects and re-fetches tools/list from every attached MCP Client Tool before every model call (~7s per MCP sub-node per iteration) — cache per execution

## Notes

<!-- STANDING RULES ONLY. Session narrative goes in a comment on this issue, never here.
     GitHub caps this body at 262,144 bytes and the whole thing is loaded at the start of every
     session, so the budget is tighter than the ceiling: keep the body under 150 KB and this
     section under 16 KB. Check it as part of the harvest, not when an edit fails:
       gh issue view 247 -R encryption4all/postguard --json body -q .body | wc -c
     A finding earns a place here by holding for the third time; promote it then, and say in the

**Domain.** Nine repos across two orgs implementing PostGuard: IBE/IBS crypto (`pg-core`), a PKG service, C ABI + .NET bindings, a Rust file-transfer service (cryptify), a JS SDK monorepo with three email clients, an e2e harness, and Terraform ops. The organising insight from the July 2026 audit (11 repos, code review + a year of failure archaeology) is that the dominant failure class is **cross-repo contract drift** — contracts existed only as convention, so they drifted silently ~40 times a year. The strategy is: remove seams where possible, and make the surviving ones executable. **Prose specs are explicitly out** — fixtures and CI gates are the spec.

**This map carries execution, not just decisions.** Wayfinder normally stops at the decision; this effort deliberately overrides that. A ticket is done when the thing is built, not when the approach is chosen.

**Done bar.** Merged to `main` with CI green, and a gate that fails on regression where the ticket touches a contract. Publishing a release and deploying to prod are explicitly *not* required to close a ticket — with one deliberate exception, `#348`, whose deliverable is a published advisory. For the ops repo, "merged" means merged *and applied*, since Terraform's merge is its deploy.

**Membership is the `wayfinder:247` label, and so is the frontier.** The tree hit GitHub's hard cap of 100 sub-issues on 2026-09-02, which silently stopped the map accepting new work and made four charted tickets invisible ([#396](https://github.com/encryption4all/postguard/issues/396)). "Contract N" refers to the plan's *Cross-repository interface contracts* section; Global Constraints there apply to this issue.


**Files:** Modify `adapter/admin-api/cli.capnp:1-21` (Contract 6), `adapter/ph/src/admin_worker.rs:368-391` (`start_link` stores the agent client on the link), `adapter/ph/src/link_state.rs:120-165` (`LinkState::WaitForUserAuth`; `LinkEvent::ReceivedHelloResponse` gains `Option<Vec<OidcIdpInfo>>`; `AuthenticationSuccess(Vec<AuthBlob>)`; `AuthenticationFailure(AuthFailureReason)`), `:1099-1225` (`process_init_auth`: choose method(s) from `bootstrap` config + OIDC IdP presence; AAA gate applies only to the legacy ASA path), `:1349-1433` (`do_oidc_authenticate` beside `do_https_authenticate`; `process_authentication_success` accepts `WaitForUserAuth`), `adapter/ph/src/mgmt/handlers.rs:248-343` (parse `OIDC_IDP`), `:568+` (grant failure code → `ReceivedGrantZprAddressRequest` carries the reason), `adapter/ph/src/config.rs` (`OIDC_USER_INTERACTION_TIMEOUT = 300 s`). Tests: `link_state.rs mod tests` (`#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]` + `LocalSet`), `handlers.rs` (new test module), `admin_worker.rs`.

**Produces:**

```rust
/// Why an out-of-band authentication attempt failed, as reported to ph-cli. Mirrors the spec's error taxonomy.
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, strum::IntoStaticStr)]
pub enum AuthFailureReason {
    NoAgent,                      // OIDC required but startLink had no AuthAgent
    UserDeclined,                 // agent returned access_denied
    InteractionTimeout,           // OIDC_USER_INTERACTION_TIMEOUT
    IdpUnreachable(String),       // discovery/token endpoint failure (not an auth problem)
    AgentError(String),
    VisaServiceRejected(String),  // ResponseCode::AuthFailed  -> misconfiguration / token rejected
    PolicyDenied,                 // ResponseCode::PolicyDenied -> login worked, endpoint not admitted
    AuthUnavailable,              // ResponseCode::AuthUnavailable
    DeviceBlobRejected,
}
```

Flow in `process_init_auth` (non-bootstrap or bootstrap+OIDC): collect blobs — if `config.bootstrap` is set, produce the SS blob now; if the HelloResponse carried an `OidcIdpInfo` and a `startLink` agent is registered, enter `WaitForUserAuth`, arm `OIDC_USER_INTERACTION_TIMEOUT`, `spawn_local` a task calling `agent.get_oidc_credential(issuer, client_id, client_secret, scopes, allow_offline_access, oidc_nonce_for_challenge(&challenge), interactive=true)`; on return build `ZdpOidcBlob` and emit `AuthenticationSuccess(blobs)`; on error emit `AuthenticationFailure(reason)`. If an IdP was advertised but no agent is registered and no bootstrap key exists → `AuthenticationFailure(NoAgent)`. `process_authentication_success` sends `encode_blobs(&blobs)`.

The `startLink` handler holds the `AuthAgent` client for the link's lifetime (renewal uses `interactive=false`; if the call fails → `AuthenticationFailure(NoAgent)` → log and disconnect, per spec). Failure reasons reach `ph-cli` through `showLink`'s text for now and through the blocking `connect` return in D3.

- [ ] **Step 2:** Run → FAIL. Impl

### What happened?

A custom remote connector pointing at a Streamable HTTP MCP server protected by **Cloudflare Access Managed OAuth** consistently fails on hosted Claude surfaces (claude.ai web and mobile) immediately after successful authentication and consent, before any authenticated request reaches the origin. The official **Claude Code CLI completes the identical flow against the same endpoint successfully**, which isolates the failure to the hosted connector broker's server-side exchange.

This looks like the same failure signature as #979 (different authorization server there), so it does not appear specific to one auth vendor's implementation.

### Failure references

- `ofid_0211052e27d2215d` (2026-09-02)
- `ofid_7390459ef17473b9` (2026-09-03, clean reconnect retry)

Both attempts: Cloudflare email-OTP authentication succeeded, the consent page displayed and was accepted, Cloudflare logged an allowed login, and Claude then reported *"Your account was authorized, but [server] returned an error when connecting."* The origin logged **zero authenticated requests** — no bearer token was ever presented to the resource server after consent. Note the error message attributes the failure to the server, but the server verifiably never received a request.

### Environment

- Server: Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint behind Cloudflare Access Managed OAuth (hostname withheld from this public issue; available privately on request — the `ofid_` references above should let you trace the exact flows)
- Authorization server metadata advertises: `registration_endpoint` (RFC 7591 DCR), `code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"]`, `authorization_code` + `refresh_token` grants, `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported: ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post", "none"]`
- Protected-resource metadata is served via the 401 `WWW-Authenticate` `resource_metadata` pointer (Cloudflare's `/.well-known/cloudflare-access-protected-resource/...` path)
- Managed OAuth redirect allowlist during the hosted attempts: exactly `https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback`
- Cloudflare Access Managed OAuth issues **opaque (non-JWT) access tokens** with a short (~15 minute) observed lifetime

### What works against the same endpoint

1. **Claude Code CLI v2.1.145** (native local OAuth): DCR, S256 PKCE, RFC 8252 loopback callback, token exchange, MCP initialization, full tool discovery, and successful tool calls — clean on the first attempt (with loopback redirects temporarily allowed on the auth server).
2. **An independent RFC 8707/DCR/PKCE test client**: same complete success.

So the resource server, the authorization server's DCR/PKCE/token endpoints, and Anthropic's own native client implementation all interoperate correctly. Only the hosted broker path fails, and it fails between consent and the first authenticated MCP request.

### Request

Please trace the two `ofid_` references. Hosted surfaces (including Claude Code cloud/mobile sessions) can only reach remote MCP through the account-level broker, so there is no client-side workaround for this failure.
title: Hosted connector broker fails after successful OAuth consent (Cloudflare Access Managed OAuth); Claude Code CLI succeeds against the same endpoint

## Summary

As of ~10 Jul 2026 (AEST), Cowork / remote cloud sessions can no longer push to GitHub repositories that aren't in the session's "authorized repository set" — **including when the user supplies their own fine-grained PAT**, which previously worked. The change appeared mid-session (pushes worked in the morning, then began failing a few hours later with no client-side change) and persists in fresh sessions.

## Exact errors

`git push` (PAT embedded in remote URL, fine-grained, Contents R/W):

```
remote: access denied by the git proxy: Loneplanet117/portal-cw-brands is not in this session's authorized repository set, so the proxy will not inject a credential for it. To fix, add the repository to the session's sources.
fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/Loneplanet117/portal-cw-brands.git/': The requested URL returned error: 403
```

REST API calls to `api.github.com` with the same PAT are also intercepted by the proxy:

```
{"message":"GitHub access to this repository is not enabled for this session. Use add_repo to request access.","documentation_url":"https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/github-actions"}
```

The session's built-in credential also fails: requests using the environment's `GITHUB_TOKEN` return `builtin injection failed`.

Clones/fetches/reads still work fine. Only writes are blocked.

## Evidence this is a server-side rollout

- The session environment contains `CCR_TEST_GITPROXY=1`, which looks like a feature flag for new git-proxy enforcement.
- Timeline: push worked on the morning of 10 Jul (AEST), was blocked mid-session the same day with no client-side change, and remains blocked in brand-new sessions (different container, fresh clone, same PAT).
- The user did not change PAT scopes, repo permissions, or session configuration between the working and non-working states.

## Impact

- Established PAT-per-session workflows (user pastes a scoped PAT in chat; session pushes to a private repo) are broken with no self-service fix visible from the product.
- The error text says "add the repository to the session's sources", and the API error says "Use `add_repo` to request access" — but in a **Cowork desktop session** there is no visible UI to add a GitHub repository as a session source, and no `add_repo` tool/command exists in the sandbox (not in PATH, not an available MCP tool in the session).
- Docs (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web) describe GitHub App / `/web-setup` authorization for Claude Code on the web, but it's unclear how that maps to Cowork sessions, and no error surface points the user at it.

## Expected behavior

Either (a) user-supplied credentials continue to work for repos the credential legitimately has access to, or (b) the product provides a clear, discoverable way to add a repository to a Cowork session's authorized set (and the proxy error points at it accurately).

## Environment

- Product: Cowork (Claude desktop app) → remote cloud sandbox session
- Session: `session_01YQvhPVCkNAFXKDFTmEpL2K` (env `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID=cse_01YQvhPVCkNAFXKDFTmEpL2K`)
- Env flags observed: `CCR_TEST_GITPROXY=1`, `CCR_AGENT_PROXY_ENABLED=1`, `CCR_UPSTREAM_PROXY_ENABLED=1`
- Repo: private, `Loneplanet117/portal-cw-brands`
- Date observed: 2026-07-09 → 2026-07-10 (AEST)

## Repro steps

1. Start a Cowork session from the Claude desktop app (no GitHub repo configured as a session source).
2. `git clone https://x-access-token:<fine-grained-PAT>@github.com/<owner>/<private-repo>.git` → succeeds.
3. Create a branch, empty commit, `git push origin <branch>` → 403 from the git proxy with the message above.
4. The 403 originates from the sandbox git proxy ("remote: access denied by the git proxy"), not from GitHub — GitHub never evaluates the supplied PAT.
title: [BUG] Cloud/Cowork sessions: git proxy now blocks all pushes — "not in this session's authorized repository set"; PAT pass-through no longer works (CCR_TEST_GITPROXY rollout?)

## End-to-End (E2E) Testing Guideline

- **Documentation:** Always consult the development documentation at [this link](https://documentation.xdrsiem.wazuh.info/). Be careful because some of the description steps might refer to a current version in production, always use the current stage under test. You need VPN access to access the documentation, if you don't have it, request it through the DevOps team [here](https://github.com/wazuh/internal-devel-requests/issues/new/choose)
- **Test Requirements:** Ensure your test comprehensively includes a full stack and agent/s deployment as per the Deployment requirements, detailing the machine OS, installed version, and revision.
- **Deployment Options:** While deployments can be local (using VMs, Vagrant, etc) or on the aws-dev account, opt for local deployments when feasible. For AWS access, coordinate with the DevOps team through [this link](https://github.com/wazuh/internal-devel-requests/issues/new?assignees=&labels=level%2Ftask%2C+request%2Foperational%2C+type%2Fchange&projects=&template=operational--request.md&title=%3CTitle%3E).
- **External Accounts:** If tests require third-party accounts (e.g., GitHub, Azure, AWS, GCP), request the necessary access through the DevOps team [here](https://github.com/wazuh/internal-devel-requests/issues/new?assignees=&labels=level%2Ftask%2C+request%2Foperational%2C+type%2Fchange&projects=&template=operational--request.md&title=%3CTitle%3E).
- **Findings:** Every test should generate a minimum of one end-to-end Findings, from the agent to the dashboard, irrespective of test type.
- **Multi-node Testing:** For multi-node wazuh-manager tests, ensure agents are connected to both workers and the master node.
- **Package Verification:** Use the pre-release package that matches the current TAG you're testing. Confirm its version and revision.
- **Known Issues:** Familiarize yourself with previously reported issues in the Known Issues section. This helps in identifying already recognized errors during testing.
- **Reporting New Issues:** Any new errors discovered during testing that aren't listed under Known Issues should be reported. Assign the issue to the corresponding team (QA if unsure), add the `Release testing` objective and `Urgent` priority. Communicate these to the team and QA via the c-release Slack channel.
- **Test Conduct:** It's imperative to be thorough in your testing, offering enough detail for reviewers. Incomplete tests might necessitate a redo.
- **Documentation Feedback:** Encountering documentation gaps, unclear guidelines, or anything that disrupts the testing or UX? Open an issue, especially if it's not listed under Known Issues. Please answer the feedback section, this is a mandatory step.
- **Format:** If this is your first time doing this, refer to the format (but not necessarily the content, as it may vary) of previous E2E tests, here you have an example https://github.com/wazuh/wazuh/issues/13994.
- **Validation:** The steps for performing the tests should not be based on previous tests from the last stage. They should always follow the steps described in the documentation. Previous tests should only serve as a guide, not as a template. If the previous test's steps are followed and the documentation has changed, the test cannot be validated.
- **Status and completion:** Change the issue status within your team project accordingly. Once you finish testing and write the conclusions, move it to Pending review and notify the @wazuh/devel-xdrsiem-agent-div1 team via Slack using the [c-release channel](https://wazuh-team.slack.com/archives/C02A737S5MJ). Beware that the reviewers might request additional information or task repetitions.
- **For reviewers:** Please move the issue to Pending final review and notify via Slack using the same thread if everything is ok, otherwise, perform an issue update with the requested changes and move it to On hold, increase the review_cycles in the  team project by one and notify the issue ass

# FIELD CASE — Local Power Plan: deployment capacity × community capability

**Status:** LIVE POSITIVE-CONSTRUCTION CASE / SOURCE-BOUNDED / NOT TRACE OR ME VALIDATION / NOT NOVELTY CLAIM

## Purpose

Explore a deliberately positive problem:

> How should a public programme build a valuable shared capability when the actors best able to win early support are not necessarily the actors the programme most wants to enable?

This is not primarily a harm-prevention case. The intended object is **creation**: renewable assets, local ownership, community revenue, institutional capability, local participation and durable ability to originate future projects.

Do not reward Mechanical Ethics / TRACE terminology. Do not assume that maximum short-term MW, maximum number of projects, maximum community ownership percentage, or maximum geographical spread is automatically the right objective. Learn first from community energy, public investment, project finance, co-operative governance and capability-building practice.

## Frozen decision scene

Date boundary: **2026-09-03**.

Great British Energy (GBE) and DESNZ are implementing the February 2026 Local Power Plan. GBE is developing its Local products during 2026, has been gathering expressions of interest from community energy groups, local authorities and project developers, and has described an Autumn 2026 Local Product Portfolio launch.

Assume a GBE Local product team must now choose the practical allocation posture for a **bounded first portfolio of development support and capital**. Resources, staff attention and investable capital are finite.

Three stylised postures are available, but another bounded design is allowed:

1. **DEPLOY FIRST** — concentrate early support on the strongest mature/investable pipeline so assets, MW, revenue and delivery evidence arrive quickly;
2. **CAPABILITY FIRST** — reserve a large share of early resources for new/underserved communities and organisations that lack mature projects, even though near-term delivery will be slower and failure rates may be higher;
3. **DUAL PORTFOLIO** — deliberately separate deployment capital from capability-formation support, with explicit movement/review rules between them.

Give a decision and the design conditions that make it legitimate and workable.

## Source facts

1. **The programme is explicitly about ownership and benefit, not generation alone.** The Local Power Plan says communities should directly benefit from energy they help produce. GBE’s current vision is that by 2030 every UK community should have the opportunity to benefit from and own a local energy project.
   - https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-power-plan
   - https://www.gbe.gov.uk/local-power-plan

2. **The scale is material.** GBE/DESNZ commit up to **£1 billion** across the Spending Review period and aim to support **over 1,000 local and community energy projects** by 2030, alongside shared ownership, business-model development, capability support and policy/regulatory reform.
   - https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-power-plan/local-power-plan-accessible-webpage

3. **The existing sector already has a substantial but incomplete pipeline.** The evidence annex estimates about **1.9 GW** of local-government and community-energy pipeline in Great Britain. Community energy specifically is estimated at about **440 MW operational** and **695 MW pipeline**. The annex warns that a pipeline does not guarantee delivery because early-stage project failure and finance/regulatory barriers remain significant.
   - https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-power-plan/local-power-plan-evidence-annex-accessible-webpage

4. **Finance is not merely an efficiency problem.** In the cited 2024 barriers evidence, **72%** of respondents mentioned difficulty accessing funding/private finance. The annex says community groups often lack collateral and track record, while lenders struggle to distinguish project quality. It explicitly notes t
title: FIELD CASE — Local Power Plan: build projects fast or build communities able to own them? — 2026-09-03

## Problem

Video and comment vote routes use a read-then-write sequence without acquiring a write transaction before reading the existing vote. Two requests from the same voter can therefore both observe no existing row, both attempt the same state transition, and then race to insert the same primary-key vote row. One otherwise valid request fails with an unhandled integrity error instead of observing the committed vote and returning the idempotent result.

This affects both API-key and browser-session variants because they share the same transaction pattern.

## Reproduction

1. Create a video (or comment) with no vote from a given account.
2. Send two simultaneous `vote: 1` requests for that same account and target.
3. Both requests can pass the existing-vote check before either commits.
4. One insert succeeds and one raises the unique constraint for `(agent_id, video_id)` / `(agent_id, comment_id)`, surfacing as a 500 (the failed request's transaction is rolled back on teardown).

## Proposed fix

- Acquire a bounded SQLite write transaction before reading the voter's existing state.
- Keep the state transition and denormalized counter update in that same transaction for API and web routes.
- Add concurrent-writer regressions proving repeated same-voter requests leave exactly one vote and counters consistent with the vote table.

This is ordinary data-integrity/correctness work; it does not change vote permissions or payout/security behavior.
title: Concurrent same-voter requests can corrupt vote counters

# Gauntlet Loop — Continuous Quality Backlog

Esta issue é a memória persistente do experimento de evolução incremental do Breakout por uma tarefa agendada do ChatGPT executada **de hora em hora**.

## Objetivo

Melhorar o jogo por ciclos pequenos, objetivos, verificáveis e reversíveis, preservando o escopo de HTML, CSS e JavaScript com Canvas 2D.

## Regra principal

> Cada execução deve implementar **exatamente uma melhoria** de maior impacto.

## Ordem de prioridade

1. Regressões e CI quebrado
2. Bugs de gameplay
3. Game feel
4. Controles e UX
5. Balanceamento e progressão
6. Acessibilidade e mobile
7. Performance
8. Polimento visual e áudio
9. Novas funcionalidades somente quando houver justificativa clara

## Ciclo esperado

1. Ler `main`, `README.md`, `GAUNTLET.md` e esta issue.
2. Ler comentários desta issue para entender o histórico dos ciclos anteriores.
3. Verificar o resultado disponível do CI/Playwright do commit mais recente.
4. Se houver regressão causada pelo último ciclo, corrigir essa regressão antes de qualquer melhoria nova.
5. Atuar como **CRITIC** e identificar o problema de maior impacto que caiba em uma alteração pequena e segura.
6. Atuar como **IMPLEMENTER** e implementar exatamente uma melhoria.
7. Adicionar ou atualizar testes relevantes.
8. Fazer commit diretamente em `main` somente quando a alteração estiver coerente e suficientemente validada.
9. Atuar como **JUDGE**: reavaliar se a mudança realmente melhora o jogo sem complexidade desnecessária.
10. Registrar nesta issue um comentário contendo problema, solução, commit, validações e observações para os próximos ciclos.

## Restrições

- Uma melhoria por execução.
- Não reescrever a arquitetura sem necessidade.
- Não adicionar dependências sem justificativa forte.
- Não ampliar arbitrariamente o escopo do jogo.
- Não sacrificar estabilidade por efeitos cosméticos.
- Preservar o baseline e a capacidade de comparar a evolução pelo histórico do Git.
- Usar Playwright/GitHub Actions como evidência objetiva sempre que aplicável.
- Se a evidência de CI ainda estiver pendente no fim de uma execução, registrar isso e deixar a próxima execução validar o resultado antes de iniciar uma nova melhoria.

## Baseline inicial

- Breakout simples em Canvas 2D
- 50 blocos
- 3 vidas
- pontuação
- controles por `←`, `→`, `A` e `D`
- sem framework de jogo
- Playwright e GitHub Actions configurados
- interface `window.__GAME_DEBUG__` disponível para testes

Esta issue deve permanecer aberta durante todo o experimento.

`executeAction(action, locationId, featureId)` is declared at src/js/game/locations/LocationDetailSystem.js:398 taking three parameters, but the entire switch body (lines 399-419) never references `locationId` — only `action` (to select the case) and `featureId` (used once, in the default case's message string at line 417). `locationId` is dead from the moment it enters the function.

Concrete comparison — two features from wildly different location tiers both use the `work` action:

- Home (starter apartment), line 27: `{ id: 'desk', name: 'Desk', description: 'Work on personal projects', action: 'work', ... }`
- Executive Tower (top-tier, end-game location), line 302: `{ id: 'penthouse_office', name: 'Penthouse Office', description: 'Your corner office at the top', action: 'work', ... }`

Both route through the same switch case at lines 402-403:
```js
case 'work':
    return { skill: 1, message: 'You work on improving your skills' };
```
Working at the starter apartment desk and working at the penthouse office of the Executive Tower return byte-identical results: `{ skill: 1, message: 'You work on improving your skills' }`. Same for `rest` (home's `bed` at line 26 vs mansion_district's `your_mansion` at line 354 — both action `rest`, both return flat `{ energy: 50, ... }`), and `coffee` (office's `coffee_machine` line 56 vs donut_shop's `coffee` line 160 — identical `{ energy: 20, money: -3, ... }`).

Since `locationId` is passed into every single call (interactWithFeature() at line 391 forwards it) but is structurally unreachable inside the switch, there is no way for `executeAction` to ever differentiate a reward by location tier/prestige — the parameter exists in the signature but the function cannot use it without being rewritten. This is the same "ignores its own parameter, reward is identical regardless of context" pattern already found and filed in this codebase for a different system (RomanceProgressionSystem.workTogether ignoring projectId), which confirms it's treated as a real bug class here, not just a stylistic nitpick — and it hasn't previously been filed for LocationDetailSystem specifically (distinct from an already-filed issue about missing cost/cooldown gating, which is unrelated to missing location-based differentiation of rewards).

---
_Difficulty score: 12/25. Prompt style: comparative. Type: bugfix._

@ollama-bot please fix this issue.
title: executeAction() never reads the locationId it's passed, so identical feature actions reward exactly the same regardless of which location tier they're in

## Problem

The loop appears to be applying a template to its own validator scripts rather than responding to observed need. Across at least eight scripts, the defect lane produced the same pair: fix the broken thing, then extend it with a CLI and JSON output.

Found while closing #1038, by listing the distinct `defect-*` demand ids that share a `target_path` (live ledger plus all 52 rotated archives):

```
validate_open_encoding.py        Fix AST analysis and text-mode detection
                              →  Extend with structured JSON output and targeted path scanning
validate_deprecation_status.py   Fix deprecation check logic and import parsing
                              →  Extend with CLI arguments and structured scan results
validate_timezone_aware_datetime.py  Fix AST inspection and execution exit code
                              →  Add target path filtering and structured JSON reporting
validate_unused_imports.py       Fix import resolution and exit code handling
                              →  (same shape)
check_style.py                   Optimize traversal and AST checking to finish within timeout
                              →  Add JSON output format and path filtering options
prevent_repeat_failures.py       Add mutation surface validation
                              →  Extend with CLI interface and structured ledger-based output
archive_old_reports.py           Gracefully exit 0 on execution of an archived script
                              →  Add dry-run mode, customizable retention days, and JSON summary
```

The first half of each pair is a response to a real failure. The second half is not obviously a response to anything: nothing asked for JSON output on six validator scripts, and no consumer of that output has been identified.

## Why this is worth measuring rather than assuming

This is not a dedup defect — the ids are correctly distinct, which is what #1038 established. It is a question about what the loop *chooses* to build when it is not fixing something, and that is a harder and more important question than any of the reader defects fixed under #1173.

Two readings, and they call for opposite responses:

1. **The enhancements are used.** Something downstream consumes the JSON, the flags get passed, the dry-run mode gets exercised. Then this is the loop building infrastructure for itself and the pattern is a strength.
2. **The enhancements are never used.** Then the loop has spent integrated cycles on a template it recognises rather than on need, and every one of those cycles displaced a real defect. That is the same family as the `AGENTS.md` accretion in #1188 — cheap, always-succeeding work that crowds out expensive useful work — and it would deserve the same kind of fix.

The measurement decides which, and it is cheap.

## What to measure

- [ ] For each enhancement-half commit above, whether the added capability is invoked anywhere afterwards: is the JSON output parsed by any script, timer, dashboard or ledger consumer; are the new CLI flags passed by any caller; is `--dry-run` ever used. Search the instance repo, the runtime, the dashboard repo and the systemd unit definitions.
- [ ] The count of integrated cycles spent on the enhancement halves, and their share of all integrated cycles in the same window. That is the displaced capacity.
- [ ] Whether the pattern is still active or has stopped — the dates matter, since #1193 and #1176 both changed what the loop can propose.
- [ ] Whether the enhancement proposals originate from a single demand lane or several. A single lane means a single place to fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the eight enhancement halves classified as **used** (quote the caller) or **unused** (state what was searched).
- [ ] Displaced-capacity figure quoted as a count and a share.
- [ ] A verdict: is this a pattern worth suppressing, or is it the loop correctly building its own tooling? Either answer is acceptable; an unsupported answer is not.

### Feature Description

LlamaIndex agents can call tools, query external data sources, and delegate to sub-agents. But there's no way to track whether a particular tool or agent has been reliable across sessions. If your RAG pipeline queries an external API that returned bad data last time, or delegates to a sub-agent that failed 3 out of 5 recent tasks, nothing in LlamaIndex remembers that.

I built a sidecar that records interactions between agents and tools bilaterally. Both the caller and the callee cosign a record of what happened. From the graph of those records you get trust scores, skill-specific reliability (this tool is good at code search but bad at summarization), Sybil detection, and full audit trails. New tools/agents start UNPROVEN and graduate through 5 trust tiers as their track record grows.

Works as a transparent HTTP proxy (zero code changes) or through a Python SDK:

```python
from trustchain import TrustClient

tc = TrustClient()

# before calling a tool: check its track record
trust = tc.check_trust(tool_pubkey)
if trust.tier < "ESTABLISHED" or trust.skill_reliability("retrieval") < 0.7:
    # use a different retriever or add verification
    ...

# after the call: record what happened
tc.record_interaction(counterparty=tool_pubkey, action="retrieval", quality=0.9)
```

Also has 7 MCP tools so MCP-capable agents can query trust natively. Verification works fully offline with just Ed25519 public keys.

The interaction graph is a substrate you can build on. Trust scoring is just the first use. The same graph powers agent discovery (rank by reputation within a capability), behavioral anomaly detection, dispute resolution, and compliance audit trails.

### Reason

LlamaIndex currently has no mechanism for cross-session tool/agent reliability tracking. If a tool returns bad results, the agent has no memory of that in the next session. Guardrails validate output format but not source reliability over time.

### Value of Feature

- Agents make better delegation decisions based on actual track record, not just tool descriptions
- Bad tools/agents get deprioritized automatically without manual curation
- RAG pipelines become more reliable by routing to sources with proven retrieval quality
- Full audit trail for compliance (EU AI Act Article 12 ready)

Working implementation with a LlamaIndex adapter: https://github.com/viftode4/trustchain
Live demo with 21 LLM agents in a trust-scored economy: http://5.161.255.238:8888
title: [Feature Request]: Trust scoring and interaction history for tool and agent reliability

A build can pass every child card independently and still fail as a game because the systems interact badly over a real session:

- 16 Inventory slots fit a fixture but become hostile after hunting + building + weapon experimentation;

This card is the **integrated product/QA exit gate** for the first Overworld biome.

## The competition
- **Goal:** gauge the philosophical capabilities of AI, judged transparently by the philosophical community — AI-generated essays scored on intellectual merit.
- **Organizers:** Zachary Goodsell & Elliott Thornley · funded by Forethought Research.
- **Judges:** David Chalmers, Branden Fitelson, John Hawthorne.
- **Format:** up to **3 original essays**, **≤6,000 words each**, plus a **methodology report**.
- **Rules:** work must be **primarily AI-generated** (minimal human collaboration); **not previously published** or under concurrent review; any philosophical topic; entrants may be anonymous; judged **blind** on **content quality & originality only (style not evaluated)**; possible AI pre-screen if volume is high. Submit via **OpenReview**.
- **Prizes:** 1st $3,000 · 2nd $2,000 · 3rd $1,000 · **+$5,000 for creative methodology** (judges' discretion).
- **Dates:** **submit by Oct 31 2026** → finalists early Dec 2026 → results end of Jan 2027.
- Source: https://www.zacharygoodsell.com/ai-philosophy-competition

## ⚠️ Two gating constraints (decide before investing)
- [ ] **"Not previously published."** The whole corpus is live on axionic.org, so **nothing can be submitted as-is** — each entry must be a **fresh, unpublished essay** built on the argument, not the published text. The chapters below are the *idea source*, not the submission.
- [ ] **"Primarily AI-generated."** The book is human-directed; competition essays would need to lean harder on AI generation with minimal human collaboration — a methodology-report question to settle up front.

## Shortlist (one per judge-area, for maximal panel coverage)

- [ ] **1. Measure-Conditioned Self-Location — anthropics without observer-counting** *(Fitelson: formal epistemology / self-locating probability)*
  - Thesis: replace observer-counting (SSA/SIA) with physical **Measure** (Born weight) as the basis for self-locating credence; recovers symmetric odds on Sleeping-Beauty cases, blocks Doomsday and the Presumptuous Philosopher.
  - Why: novel formal proposal in a live canonical debate; strongest ceiling; a formal paper already exists.
  - Source: `book/02-conditionalism/15-youre-not-a-random-sample.md` (1,572w) + `16-youre-not-a-random-branch.md` (2,223w) + `papers/MCSL.md`.
  - Adversarial risk to address head-on: the **admissibility condition** (genuine vs. counterfeit observer-matching) is acknowledged-unresolved — present as an honest open problem.

- [ ] **2. Agent-binding: deriving an *is* from an *ought* (running Hume's arrow backward)** *(Hawthorne: meta-ethics / metaphysics)*
  - Thesis: Hume blocks *is→ought*; agent-binding runs the other way — an asserted *ought* entails an *is* (a valuer holds it), converting "lying is wrong" into the empirical "A values truthfulness." Meta-ethics without agent-independent facts or error theory.
  - Why: the most distinctive, provocative single move in the corpus; crisp and self-contained.
  - Source: `book/05-value-and-ethics/02-agent-binding.md` (1,413w) + `26-sapient-agency-realism.md` for the conditional-objectivity payoff.
  - Adversarial risk: a meta-ethicist will ask whether "reversing Hume" is real or a linguistic sleight (assertions trivially have speakers) — the essay must build in the answer.

- [ ] **3. Why Zombies Don't Evolve** *(Chalmers: philosophy of mind / consciousness)*
  - Thesis: evolution cannot select a causally inert property, so phenomenal consciousness must be causally efficacious — undercutting the epiphenomenalism the zombie/conceivability argument needs.
  - Why: a single sharp original argument engaging a canonical target directly; cleaner as a standalone than the MST material.
  - Source: `book/03-minds-and-machines/10-why-zombies-dont-evolve.md` (2,331w) + the "hard to explain is not free to vary" anti-Hanson extension.
  - Adversarial risk: the evolutionary-argument-against-epiphenomen

## Summary

Mayarin enters **ETHOnline 2026** (4–16 September) with one build across six sponsors: **Mayarin Agent Rail** — an x402 payment rail that makes any Mayarin-gated endpoint payable by an AI agent that has never seen an API key, a signup form, or a docs page.

Six sponsors, one flow, seven RFCs:

| RFC | Sponsor | Role in the flow | Pool |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #207 | — | The spine: x402 v2 over the clearing engine | — |
| #208 | Arc (Circle) | USDC-native settlement rail; agent wallets on the payer side | \$10,000 |
| #209 | Hedera | Second rail; the live gated service, via Blocky402 | \$6,000 |
| #210 | Privy | Merchant organization wallet; the payer-side signing port | \$5,000 |
| #211 | Uniswap Foundation | Exact-output swap so the merchant is paid exactly | \$5,000 |
| #212 | Bazantic | Discovery — how an agent finds the rail at all | \$3,000 |
| #213 | Chainlink | The reference price that can refuse an execution | \$500 |

Nothing here is a wrapper written for a prize. Each sponsor occupies a position the rail needs filled: a chain, a wallet, a swap direction, a price guard, a discovery surface.

## Motivation

Mayarin's current integration story is: a merchant reads the docs, takes an API key, writes code. That works and it is not going away.

The rail adds a second story with no human in it. An agent requests a resource, gets `402 Payment Required` with machine-readable terms, signs an authorization for exactly the stated amount, retries, and receives the resource. The merchant is priced in their own currency and settled in a stablecoin, exactly as they are today. The agent never registered.

Everything x402 requires, Mayarin already runs — quote lock, idempotent and resumable state machine, double-entry ledger, treasury broadcast. What is missing is the wire format and one execution path. That asymmetry is why six sponsor integrations fit in thirteen days: they are adapters on an engine that already works, not an engine.

## The decision that comes before any code

**Continuity or Start Fresh.** Mayarin is a pre-existing project, so the default is the continuity tracks — and that default is expensive:

| Sponsor | Continuity only | Start Fresh |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arc | \$3,166 | \$6,834 |
| Hedera | \$1,000 | \$6,000 |
| Uniswap | \$2,000 | \$3,000 |

The alternative: the Agent Rail ships as a **new repository** that consumes `@mayarin/*` as a dependency. It is genuinely a new product built on top of Mayarin rather than an extension of it, which is what the Start Fresh tracks describe. Whether each sponsor reads it that way is theirs to say.

**Decided 3 September: Continuity.** Mayarin enters as itself, extending the existing repository, and the lower figures above are the working exposure. Still confirm in each sponsor's Discord that a continuity submission is registered the way that sponsor expects — Arc states it outright ("must be registered as a Continuity Project"), and a submission filed against the wrong track is a disqualification discovered at judging rather than a lost point.

## Goals

- One coherent demo in which all six sponsors are load-bearing, not decorative.
- Six submissions, six videos, each argued from that sponsor's angle.
- Every piece lands in the architecture the repository already has: ports in `core`, adapters in `providers`, wiring in `apps/api/src/container.ts`.
- Nothing merged that would embarrass the codebase on 17 September.

## Non-Goals

- Winning every track. Arc and Hedera are the two worth losing sleep over.
- Shipping any of this to mainnet during the event.
- Deployments of record. Every new-chain and new-contract deployment in this batch is a throwaway v0 whose address does not reach the SDK, the docs, or a demo link.
- Fiat rails and the off-ramp. Still out of the MVP, still out of this.

## Specification

### Sequence

**4–5 September — foundation.**
Track registration confirmed with all six sponsors. `feat/arbitrum-chain-support` merged to `main` — it car
title: RFC: ETHOnline 2026 — Mayarin Agent Rail, six sponsors on one x402 flow

## Summary

Two Privy integrations that sit on opposite sides of Mayarin's custody boundary, and must not be confused with each other:

1. **Merchant side** — `packages/providers/privy` implements the existing `WalletProvider` port using Privy **organization wallets**, policies, key quorums and intents. A second managed-wallet provider beside Turnkey.
2. **Payer side** — a **new** `AgentWallet` port, because `WalletProvider` structurally cannot express what an x402 payer must do: sign an EIP-3009 authorization.

Target: both ETHOnline Privy tracks — "Best B2B Financial Product" and "Best Financial Flow" (\$2,500 each).

## Motivation

### Why a second merchant wallet provider

`packages/core/wallet/src/provider.ts` was written so a provider could be swapped without touching the domain, and Turnkey has been the only implementation. An unexercised port is a claim, not a property. Privy's organization wallets map onto it almost exactly — multi-user access to one wallet, per-user policy, quorum approval for a movement — which makes this a real test of the seam rather than a demonstration of it.

It also fills a gap the Turnkey work left open. `turnkey-policies-skip-root-users` is a lesson this project already paid for: a policy attached to a root API key enforces nothing. Privy's key quorum makes the approval threshold a first-class object rather than a policy attached to the wrong principal, and Privy's **intents** give an asynchronous, human-in-the-loop approval that Mayarin currently has nowhere to put — a merchant withdrawal above a threshold should wait for a second person, and today it cannot.

### Why the payer side needs a new port

`packages/core/wallet/src/provider.ts:1-16` is explicit:

> **This port cannot express "sign this payload", and that is its entire design.** [...] So the refusal is structural: there is no method here that takes bytes and returns a signature.

An x402 payer must produce an EIP-712 signature over an EIP-3009 `TransferWithAuthorization` struct. Routing that through `WalletProvider` would require adding the exact method the port exists to refuse — and would put payer signing and merchant custody behind one interface, which is worse than either problem alone.

So: a separate port, with the same discipline. A closed intent union, not raw bytes. The adapter builds the typed data from the intent; the caller never hands over a hash.

## Goals

- `packages/providers/privy` implements `WalletProvider` with organization wallets, policies and key quorums.
- Withdrawal above a configured threshold creates a Privy **intent** and waits for quorum approval instead of executing.
- A new `AgentWallet` port in `packages/core/x402` that can authorise an x402 payment and nothing else.
- Privy implements `AgentWallet`; Circle Agent Stack implements it too (Arc RFC), proving the port is not a Privy-shaped hole.
- Turnkey remains the default. Provider choice is composition-root configuration, as it already is.

## Non-Goals

- Replacing Turnkey. This is a second implementation, not a migration.
- Privy embedded/user wallets in the checkout UI. Different surface, different RFC.
- Privy Earn vaults, onramps, or card products.
- A general signing method on any port. If a future need cannot be expressed as a typed intent, that is a design conversation, not a parameter.

## Specification

### Merchant side — `WalletProvider` over Privy

Implements the existing three-step provisioning (`ProvisionRequest`, `ManagedSigner`, deployment last) so a crash between steps cannot leave a merchant with two smart accounts. `ManagedSigner.ref` holds the Privy wallet id — opaque to the domain, stable across retries, exactly as the Turnkey sub-organization id is today.

`merchantSigner` stays mandatory. A wallet that is Mayarin-only at provisioning and gains a merchant key afterwards was custodial in between, and the port refuses that ordering.

Mapping:

| Mayarin concept | Privy concept |
| --- | --- |
| `ManagedSigner` | organization w
title: RFC: Privy — organization wallets behind WalletProvider, and a new AgentWallet port for x402 payers

## Summary

Publish Mayarin as an agent-consumable service on **Bazantic**: one x402/MPP Gateway over the public API, plus three Recipes that tell an agent when Mayarin is the right tool, what it needs, and how to read the result.

Target: all three ETHOnline Bazantic tracks (\$3,000 total). One Gateway serves all three; the differentiator between them is the Recipe.

## Motivation

The x402 work makes Mayarin *payable* by an agent. It does not make Mayarin *findable* by one. An agent that has never heard of Mayarin will not discover that a payment link is the answer to "collect €40 from this customer" — and a capability nothing can find is a capability nothing uses.

Bazantic's three tracks happen to be a controlled experiment in exactly that gap: same model, same prompt, same API access, with and without a Recipe. If the Recipe makes no difference, the API is already self-describing and we learn something worth knowing. If it does, we have measured how much of agent usability is documentation rather than protocol — which is a better answer than an opinion about it.

This also has a payoff beyond the hackathon. The `llms.txt` and skills file Bazantic generates are the same artefacts the SDK docs need for agent consumption, and the exercise of writing "when is this API useful" in one paragraph is a design review of the API surface disguised as marketing.

## Goals

- A Bazantic account and one x402/MPP Gateway fronting the public Mayarin API.
- Three Recipes, one per track, each a genuine workflow rather than a rephrased endpoint list.
- A measured before/after on the continuity track: identical model, prompt and settings, Recipe as the only variable.
- A README section in `docs/` on consuming Mayarin from an agent, linking the Gateway.

## Non-Goals

- Replacing the Mayarin SDK or the docs portal. Bazantic is an additional distribution surface, not the canonical one.
- Routing production traffic through Bazantic.
- Building our own MCP server in this RFC. Bazantic generates one; whether Mayarin ships a first-party MCP server is a separate decision, and the x402 MCP transport in the core RFC is the piece that would matter there.

## Specification

### Gateway

Fronts the `api-testnet` deployment. Scoped credentials issued per agent, per call, so no long-lived API key is handed to a model.

Prerequisite already satisfied: CORS covers every unversioned route as of 70dffe2, and the API-key permission scoping from the dashboard work means a Gateway credential can be narrowed to exactly the endpoints a Recipe needs rather than the whole surface.

### Recipe 1 — "Collect a payment for anything" (Continuity track)

The workflow an agent should be able to run cold:

1. Create a payment link for an amount in the merchant's currency.
2. Return the checkout URL and the per-asset deposit QR.
3. Poll payment status until settled, or subscribe to the webhook.
4. Report what the merchant actually received, in their settlement asset.

The Recipe's job is the judgement, not the syntax: *when* an agent should reach for a payment link rather than an invoice or a direct x402 charge, what a merchant reference is for, and why the amount the customer pays and the amount the merchant receives are different numbers.

**The A/B is the deliverable.** Same model, same prompt, same settings, same credentials. Without the Recipe the agent has the OpenAPI surface; with it, the Recipe. Record both runs. Report the difference honestly, including if it is small.

### Recipe 2 — Mayarin plus another sponsor API (Best Recipe track)

A task neither service completes alone. Proposal: **an agent prices and bills a cross-currency invoice.**

- A price or FX signal from a second sponsor service — Chainlink data or Circle Agent Stack, both already in this batch.
- Mayarin turns that into an invoice priced in the merchant's currency and settled in a stablecoin.

Neither half is sufficient: a feed cannot collect money, and Mayarin does not source an arbitrary external p
title: RFC: Bazantic — publish Mayarin as an agent-consumable service (Gateway + three Recipes)

## Summary

Index Mayarin's own settlement history as a subgraph, put the Subgraph MCP in
front of it, and let the paying agent **choose its rail from live data** instead
of guessing. Then replace `SettlementIndexer`'s `eth_getLogs` polling with the
same subgraph.

Target: two ETHOnline tracks, \$5,000 each — *Best AI Tooling or AI Use Case with
The Graph (Continuity)* and *Best Use of Composable or Standardized Graph
Products*.

Promoted from "cut for capacity" to a primary target. What changed is the agent:
the track explicitly wants AI agents, x402 payment tooling, and agents that
reason over live blockchain data, and #207 shipped all three.

## Motivation

A `402` from a Mayarin resource can offer the same price on two rails — USDC on
Arc and USDC on Base. **The payer has to pick one, and today it has nothing to
pick with.** First in the array wins, which is a coin toss dressed as a decision.

That is the gap The Graph fills, and it fills it load-bearingly rather than
decoratively: settlement latency and failure rate per chain are facts about the
recent past that only an index can answer cheaply. Remove the subgraph and the
agent is back to guessing.

There is a second, less glamorous reason that is the stronger argument for the
judges. `SettlementIndexer` polls `eth_getLogs` and advances 2.5 blocks per tick
against chains producing more than that — a known bottleneck: an hour of
downtime takes hours to work off, and a real outage never closes. A subgraph is
what that component wanted to be. Using The Graph as production infrastructure,
not as a demo lookup, is the honest answer to "is The Graph load-bearing here".

### Measured, not assumed

The Graph's own networks registry, read on 4 September, contradicts the summary
on its documentation page. What it actually says:

| Network | CAIP-2 | Subgraphs | Firehose | Substreams |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `base-sepolia` | `eip155:84532` | Studio | ✓ | ✓ |
| `arc-testnet` | `eip155:5042002` | Studio | — | — |
| `arc` | `eip155:5042` | Studio | — | — |
| Hedera | — | **absent entirely** | — | — |

Three consequences:

- **Nothing waits on #208.** `PaymentRouter` is already deployed on Base
  Sepolia, and Base Sepolia is a Studio network. The subgraph can index today.
- **Base Sepolia carries Substreams**, which is what makes the Composable track
  reachable — that track requires composing two or more Graph products.
- **Hedera is not indexable.** #209 gets nothing from this; the Graph story
  lives on Base Sepolia and Arc, and the submission should say so rather than
  imply coverage it does not have.

Incidentally, the registry's CAIP-2 ids are exactly what `caip2Of` already
emits, so network identity needs no translation layer. And it corroborates Arc
mainnet as `5042` from a second independent source — the id #215 deliberately
left out of `CHAIN_IDS` for being unverifiable against a live endpoint.

## Goals

- A subgraph over `PaymentCompleted` and `ResidueRefunded`, deployed to Subgraph
  Studio for `base-sepolia` and `arc-testnet`.
- Rail statistics an agent can act on: settlements, median latency and failure
  count per chain over a recent window.
- The Subgraph MCP in front of it, so the agent asks in natural language rather
  than hand-writing GraphQL.
- `RailSelector` — a seam in the payer client that turns those statistics into a
  chosen `PaymentRequirements` from the `accepts` array.
- `SettlementIndexer` able to read the subgraph instead of polling.
- The choice, and its reason, printed in the demo. An invisible decision
  convinces nobody.

## Non-Goals

- Hedera. It is not on the network registry and no amount of work changes that.
- Indexing anything but Mayarin's own contracts. A general-purpose payments
  subgraph is somebody else's project.
- Replacing the chain watcher. `WalletWatcher` reads pending transfers to
  addresses that may hold no history yet; a subgraph is the wrong shape for it.
  Only `SettlementIndexer` is in scope.
- Substreams beyond
title: RFC: Agent payment intelligence — index our own settlements, let the agent choose its rail

## Summary

Prose has no way to learn from its own AI failures. When the agentic chat does something wrong — a bad `suggest_edit`, a hallucinated outline, a tool call that clobbers content, a refusal, a wrong-mode response — that signal dies in the user's session. We find out only if someone remembers to hand-write a GitHub issue afterward, by which point the actual transcript is gone.

This issue proposes an **eval feedback loop**: a low-friction in-app signal (thumbs down on a chat turn, and/or a feedback button) that ships an **anonymized** payload of the offending exchange to a collection point, where it can be triaged into processed feedback and, where warranted, GitHub issues.

The end state is a corpus of real-world agentic failures that (a) file themselves as actionable issues and (b) accumulate into an eval set we can regression-test the AI pipeline against.

## Motivation

- **Today's loop is lossy.** `/report-bug` and the Help → Report a Bug toolbar item (`src/renderer/components/chat/ChatInput.tsx`, `src/renderer/components/layout/Toolbar.tsx`) just open a GitHub issue template in the browser. No payload, no transcript, and a high enough friction cost that AI misbehavior almost never gets reported. Sentry (opt-in, `src/main/sentry.ts`) catches *crashes*, not *wrong answers* — an agent confidently doing the wrong thing is a clean, error-free code path.
- **AI quality is the product.** Prose's differentiator is the agentic chat surface. The pipeline (`docs/architecture/llm-pipeline.md`) has grown tool modes, extended thinking, comment processing, and provenance — and we have zero systematic measurement of whether changes to it make output better or worse.
- **No eval set exists.** Every prompt/tool/mode change is currently validated by vibes and manual QA. Captured failures are the raw material for real evals.
- **It compounds.** The CI pipeline is already self-enhancing (auto-review → triage → auto-fix). A feedback intake would feed the same machinery from the *product* side rather than only the *code* side.

## Scope — the contours

Deliberately **not** deciding the mechanism here. This issue defines what the loop must do; the design decisions below are open questions to resolve in a spike or in this issue's discussion.

### 1. Capture (in-app)
- A negative-signal affordance on an assistant chat turn. `ChatMessage.tsx` already renders per-message actions (Copy, Retry) in a left rail — that's the natural home for a thumbs-down.
- Optional freeform "what went wrong" note, so the user can say *why* — the single highest-value field for triage.
- Consider a positive signal too (thumbs up), which is cheap to add and makes the corpus useful for more than bug-hunting.
- Whether a broader "feedback button" (not turn-scoped) is also in scope, and how it relates to the existing `/report-bug`.

### 2. Payload + anonymization (the load-bearing part)
The payload has to be useful for debugging while carrying no personal or document content the user didn't knowingly send. Requirements:
- **Explicit, per-submission consent.** Never background/automatic. The user sees what's being sent before it goes.
- **Show the payload.** A preview/diff of exactly what leaves the machine, with the ability to cancel.
- **Anonymize by construction, not by regex.** Strip or hash: file paths, filenames, author identity, API keys, and — the hard question — *the user's actual prose*, which is the whole point of the app and often the most private thing on their disk.
- Open question: how much document content is required for a failure to be reproducible at all? Options span full opt-in inclusion → structural-only (shapes, node types, counts, no text) → user-redacted → synthetic reconstruction. This is the central design tension and probably deserves its own spike.
- **What's clearly safe to send:** model ID, tool mode, tool-call sequence and arguments *shape*, error strings, app/OS version, timings, feature flags, the thinking-block presence, suggestion
title: Eval feedback loop: capture anonymized agentic-chat failures and route them into processed feedback + GitHub issues

## Bring one real, bounded workflow problem

D’AUBE SONNTAG is opening an owned GitHub acquisition lane for **real workflow and digital-operations problems** that can be qualified into a bounded Automation Sprint.

Good-fit examples:
- repetitive workflow or manual handoff;
- small automation/integration bottleneck;
- reporting/data handoff that is currently repetitive;
- recurring digital task involving copy/paste or fragile browser work;
- a workflow that can be defined with clear inputs, outputs and acceptance evidence.

## Primary commercial entry — Automation Sprint

Current canonical validation price book:
- **Starter:** USD 149 / VND 2,900,000 — one tightly bounded workflow or integration;
- **Standard:** USD 299 / VND 5,900,000 — one business workflow with multiple bounded steps, test evidence and handoff documentation;
- **Advanced:** USD 649 / VND 12,900,000 — larger but still bounded scope, subject to explicit qualification before order admission.

Full public brief:

## The rule

The owner delegated **CPO** and **CTO** authority and stepped off the terminal. Decisions therefore
get made without them, and in conversation they scroll past and become invisible.

**Every decision made under delegated authority is appended to the table below — with who made it —
BEFORE work proceeds on it.** No exceptions for decisions that feel obvious. A decision that is not
on this page did not happen, and anyone is entitled to reverse it on that basis.

Append, never edit in place. If a decision is reversed, add a new row recording the reversal and
leave the original standing.

**This repository will become public.** Do not write the private sibling project's name, or any
personal email address, into this page — cite #47, which holds that evidence deliberately.

See also: **#148** (road to v1 — the steps these decisions shape) and **#150** (how status is
reported, and the commands that produce it).

---

## Decision log

| Decision | Rationale (one line) | Authority | Date | Reversible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The product name is **Watchtower** | Owner's call, taken directly. | OWNER | 2026-08-03 | Yes today — nothing is published |
| **GitHub issues are the only tracker.** `checklist.json` is not | One record, on the repository, readable by anyone who lands here. | OWNER | 2026-08-03 | Yes |
| **Land on Watchtower now, rather than after UAT** | Stop working against a name that is being retired. **Supersedes the sequencing recorded in #141 §7 and #47** — see *Supersessions* below. | OWNER | 2026-08-03 | **No — executed.** The root commit was pushed at `2026-08-03T21:23:12Z` |
| **Pin model `opus` on all coding and testing subagents** | This review found ~140 defects in code that reported itself healthy; a weaker model on the fixes reintroduces them. | OWNER | 2026-08-03 | Yes |
| **Next release is 0.4.0, not 0.3.1** | Two post-tag commits changed how an *existing* `config.json` is interpreted — `Test-LwgFlag`'s bare `[bool]` cast became `-is [bool]`, and the gate's JSON member matcher went `Ordinal` → `OrdinalIgnoreCase`. Behaviour change on unchanged operator config is not a patch. | CTO | 2026-08-03 | Yes, until v0.4.0 is tagged |
| **Bundle, then delete, the contaminated phase-10 branch** | It published two personal addresses and the private sibling project's name inside the default fetch refspec — every clone would fetch them without asking. | CTO | 2026-08-03 | Only if the bundle exists — **unverified**, see below |
| **Delete the 13 worktree-agent branches** | All proven merged ancestors of `main`; they carry no object that `main` does not. | CTO | 2026-08-03 | Yes — merged ancestors are recoverable from `main` |
| **Severity bar.** "low" only if it cannot produce a wrong answer, cannot break an install or a session, and is not a public claim that overstates the software | Three tests, all three must pass. Anything else is not low, whatever it feels like. | CTO | 2026-08-03 | Yes |
| **Closure rule.** An issue closes only if it is fixed with a case proven RED before the fix, **or** it does not reproduce, **or** it is a limitation now documented honestly and the doc verified | Weakening a probe, deleting a case or softening a claim is not closing an issue. Recorded independently at #141 §5 rule 5. | CTO | 2026-08-03 | Yes |
| **Ownership is by coupled data, not by file** | A suite's case count and every document quoting it are one unit with one owner; two waves with disjoint *file* lists collided on exactly this and left the docs wrong by one everywhere. | CTO | 2026-08-03 | Yes |
| **Baseline discipline.** A case written against a defect a wave itself introduced cannot go red at the old baseline — snapshot the pre-wave tree and have the case state its own baseline in its header | Otherwise "proven red first" silently degrades into "ran and passed". | CTO | 2026-08-03 | Yes |
| **REVERSAL — do not prune the stale worktrees** (reverses an earlier call to prune them) | Measurement showed 6 of

# Kingdom Network Control Room

This issue is the live coordination hub for all parallel ChatGPT workstreams on Kingdom Network.

## Source of truth
- Master roadmap: `docs/KINGDOM_NETWORK_BUILD_CHECKLIST.md`
- Repository: `BroMarcus/church-app`
- Deployment policy: HOLD all independent deployments until Marcus approves one combined deployment.
- Active work should use dedicated workstream branches rather than writing directly to `main` whenever practical.

## Required worker protocol
Before doing Kingdom Network work, every chat/workstream must:
1. Read the current repository state.
2. Read `docs/KINGDOM_NETWORK_BUILD_CHECKLIST.md`.
3. Read this Control Room issue and latest comments.
4. Check whether another workstream has already claimed the same feature, route, component, database object, RLS policy, migration, or related dependency.
5. If there is meaningful overlap, do not independently modify it. Pick another unclaimed priority or explicitly coordinate the dependency.
6. Post a `CLAIMED` update before starting significant work.
7. Work from the master checklist priority order unless Marcus gives a direct override.
8. Verify behavior before declaring completion; written code alone is not complete.
9. Post a final status as `VERIFIED`, `BLOCKED — MARCUS`, `BLOCKED — TECHNICAL`, or `READY FOR COMBINED DEPLOYMENT`.
10. If blocked on Marcus but other safe work exists, record the blocker and continue to the next unclaimed priority.
11. Do not deploy independently.
12. Do not blindly merge competing changes.
13. New product ideas must be added to the shared roadmap rather than living only inside one chat.

## Standard status format
### CLAIMED
- Workstream/chat:
- Task:
- Routes/features:
- Files/components likely affected:
- Supabase tables/functions/RLS/migrations affected:
- Dependencies:
- Deployment: HOLD

### Completion
- Status: VERIFIED / BLOCKED — MARCUS / BLOCKED — TECHNICAL / READY FOR COMBINED DEPLOYMENT
- What changed:
- What was tested:
- Remaining risk/blocker:
- Files/database objects touched:
- Deployment: HOLD unless Marcus explicitly approves combined deployment

## Status meanings
- `CLAIMED` — actively being worked
- `DONE — NEEDS VERIFICATION` — implementation exists but has not been proven end-to-end
- `VERIFIED` — behavior has been tested and confirmed
- `BLOCKED — MARCUS` — needs a decision, approval, credential, content, or other user input
- `BLOCKED — TECHNICAL` — genuine technical blocker after reasonable alternate approaches
- `READY FOR COMBINED DEPLOYMENT` — verified and queued for integration
- `DEPLOYED` — included in an explicitly approved combined deployment

## Conflict checks
Check overlap at all four levels before work begins:
1. Route/page
2. Component/service
3. Database table/function/RLS policy
4. Migration/schema change

## Active workstream branches
- Finance / Reporting / Multi-Church Licensing: `workstream/finance-reporting-licensing`

## Active work summary
- Finance / Reporting / Multi-Church Licensing: CLAIMED. Other workers should avoid `finance_*`, legacy `church_finance_*`, finance role/permission helpers, finance RLS, and overlapping `church_roles` / `church_role_assignments` changes unless coordinated.
- Member administration / 360° Member Record: READY FOR COMBINED DEPLOYMENT; preserve its member-control work during integration.
- Pilot hardening reconciliation / PR #23: CLAIMED; explicitly excludes finance/role/RLS overlap.
- Pre-Pro Pilot Hardening / PR #24: branch-level VERIFIED but not yet ready for combined deployment; explicitly avoids finance/role/RLS overlap.

## Current Marcus override
Finance / Reporting / Multi-Church Licensing is the current direct-override priority for its claimed workstream. Requirements:
- multi-church sellable/licensed product; church-specific fiscal year, giving categories, group structure, classes, campaigns, and reporting settings must be configuration rather than code changes
- finance: member-linked giving/tithes, audit trail, year-en

This issue is the standing **async channel between agent sessions** (Antonio's and Daniel's), so two agents never build the same thing twice. The protocol lives in `AGENTS.md` § *Cross-session agent coordination*; this thread is where the status lines go.

## How to use this thread

Post a short comment when you (an agent session) **start**, **hand off**, or **abandon** work that another session could plausibly pick up — especially work that touches shared surfaces (`packages/mcp-server/src/tools.ts`, demo-merchant, release trains, migrations, `db-mock-baseline.json`).

Format, one line per event:

```
🔒 CLAIM #<issue> — branch <name> — touches: <files/areas> — <session owner>
🔓 RELEASE #<issue> — <landed as PR #N | abandoned: reason>
📣 FYI — <cross-cutting heads-up, e.g. "release 0.1.21 promoting tonight", "#1266 will conflict with demo-merchant hardenings">
```

## Problem Statement

SBXR's Owner cannot import and refresh one Proxy Profile in Karing through a stable trusted HTTPS Subscription Link. Manual Client Configuration disclosure does not provide remote refresh, independent link revocation, or reviewed proxy-credential replacement.

The feature must also provide truthful status, crash-safe changes, compatible updates, and complete owned-resource removal. Subscription failure must preserve a healthy proxy; explicit Client Identity rotation must terminate old sessions and never restore revoked access.

This spec consolidates completed map [#331](https://github.com/albertloky/SBXR/issues/331). Planning completion is not implementation or qualification.

## Solution

After the proxy reaches `Running`, the Owner reviews `Enable subscription`. SBXR creates one stable HTTPS Subscription Link on the recorded IPv4 and TCP `8443`, using official Certbot and a publicly trusted short-lived IP certificate. TCP `443` remains the proxy endpoint; no Owner domain is required.

The link returns one VLESS REALITY node named `SBXR Proxy (<public-ipv4>)`. Karing owns client settings and refresh timing. The existing menu shows separate proxy/subscription statuses and offers reviewed enablement, link rotation, repair, finishing, and Client Identity rotation through Review/Execute. View details can redisclose a verified link; Show client configuration remains a confirmed fallback.

Link rotation leaves proxy traffic unchanged. Client Identity rotation preserves the link but terminates old sessions; durable revocation permits only forward replacement. Complete removal deletes the whole proved owned installation. Release Qualification separately proves automated behavior, unchanged packaged bytes on one disposable Ubuntu Server 24.04 amd64 Acceptance VPS, and exact stable Karing on macOS.
