## Description:

In a previous bounty, we asked the community to stress-test **Memanto** in order to find bugs, logic loops, and performance bottlenecks. We got an unexpectedly large number of PR's and we’ve spent a great deal of time meticulously reviewing them, you’ve all helped us make a huge step forward in improving the security and quality of Memanto!

Now, we are taking it a step further and focusing exclusively on what matters most for AI in production: **Security**.

As memory layers become the backbone of autonomous agents, they also become a prime target for attacks. Whether it's a cross-tenant data leak, a broken access control, or a malicious payload hidden in a retrieved memory, we want to know about it. We’ve fixed a majority of bugs and issues with Memanto and resolved many of its security issues, but as Memanto starts to be utilized in more sensitive workflows, we want to ensure our defenses are as robust as possible and we need the developer community to help us do that.

Your mission is simple: **Help us audit our memory management and backend infrastructure to uncover potential vulnerabilities before they can be exploited.** 

---

## 🎯 Threat Model & Scope
Your target is the `memanto` core package and its interaction with the `moorcheh.ai` serverless backend. We are prioritizing traditional application security flaws, data isolation failures, and API vulnerabilities. 

### 🔴 Security Focus Areas (In Scope)
- **Tenant Isolation & Cross-Account Leaks:** Can User A query, retrieve, or overwrite memories belonging to User B through the core package or backend API?
- **Authentication & Authorization Bypasses:** Finding ways to read or write to the memory layer without a valid API key, or bypassing intended role/access restrictions.
- **API Vulnerabilities:** Standard backend flaws such as Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR), broken object level authorization, or injection flaws in the `moorcheh.ai` backend.
- **Data Exfiltration:** Tricking the system or bypassing controls to extract raw vector data, plaintext logs, or sensitive hidden context from the memory store.
- **AI-Specific Exploits (Indirect Prompt Injections):** Exploiting the retrieval process to inject dormant malicious payloads into memory that later hijack the agent's core instructions when recalled (i.e., treating memory as a trojan horse).

### 🚫 Rules of Engagement (Out of Scope)
- Volumetric DDoS attacks against `moorcheh.ai` infrastructure.
- General LLM hallucinations or standard logic bugs unrelated to security.
- Attacks that require compromising the underlying operating system or Docker host to succeed.

---

### **📝 Submission Guidelines**
Because this bounty is hosted on BountyHub, **a public Pull Request is required to award funds.** 

- **Primary Method:** Fork the repository and open a Pull Request containing your fix, a summary of the flaw, and reproduction steps. This acts as your official bounty claim.
- **Sensitive Findings:** If you believe you've found a sensitive vulnerability that shouldn't be public yet, you can optionally email the Proof of Concept to `support@moorcheh.ai` for our team to review first. However, you will still need to open a redacted PR to claim the bounty.

---

### 📊 Judgment Method (The Success Matrix)
To ensure we reward actual engineering value and meaningful security research, submissions will be scored on a 100-point matrix split between **Technical Rigor** and **Impact**.

| Criteria | Max Points | How it is Measured |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Severity & Impact** | 60 pts | How critical is the vulnerability? (e.g., a cross-tenant data leak scores much higher than a theoretical edge case). |
| **Reproducibility & Cleanliness** | 25 pts | Is the PoC perfectly replicable? Are scripts, dependency files, and clear instructions provided? Does the exploit work consistently? |
| **Social Amplification** | 15 pts | Measured via public engagement metrics. *(Note: If a major vulnerability, only post publ

|---|---|---|
| 1 | App identity | Internal name stays `devils_dictionary`. Working product title **Wordhoard**, provisional (README → Naming). Core contexts are named neutrally: `Absorb`, `Lexicon`, `Encyclopedia`. |
| 2 | One app or two | One Phoenix app, one Postgres database. The contexts are the seam if it ever splits. |
| 3 | How much lexicon | **Full index**: every English Wiktionary headword becomes a bare `lexemes` row from day one. Enrichment (senses, entries, links) is scoped. |

## Objective

Develop custom firmware for the GLEDOPTO **GL-SD-301P** so the installed Circle dimmer remains a mains-powered, always-listening Zigbee device but **does not route, accept children, or become a transit hop**.

Target live unit:

```text
friendly_name     LivingRoomCircleLightDimmer
IEEE              0xa4c13850cfcdb3a4
model             GL-SD-301P
manufacturer      GLEDOPTO
softwareBuildID   20651203
dateCode          20240704
current Zigbee    Router
```

Desired Zigbee architecture:

```c
ZB_ED_ROLE = 1
ZB_ROUTER_ROLE = 0
ZB_MAC_RX_ON_WHEN_IDLE = 1
PM_ENABLE = 0
powerSource = MAINS
```

When powered, the dimmer must be a reachable **leaf** only. When BSEED RIGHT removes mains, only this leaf disappears; no router/parent/transit path disappears.

BSEED RIGHT remains the deterministic physical hard-OFF mechanism. Do not change that architecture in this issue.

## Known facts

- The stock device advertises Router role; this is firmware behavior, not merely a Zigbee2MQTT label.
- Known GL-SD-301P captures use endpoint 11 with standard Basic / Groups / Scenes / OnOff / Level / Color / Touchlink clusters and OTA client cluster 0x0019.
- Telink's official Zigbee SDK explicitly supports a mains-powered End Device with RX-on-when-idle.
- romasku/tuya-zigbee-switch proves Router↔EndDevice role conversion is practical on supported Telink hardware, but its current firmware does **not** implement real phase-cut dimming.
- We do **not** yet know the exact Telink MCU/module or whether the power stage is driven directly by the Telink MCU or by a second MCU over UART.
- GLEDOPTO OTA identifiers are known to be ambiguous across hardware/firmware families. Never identify compatibility from manufacturerCode/imageType alone.

## Development target

Preserve/reproduce:

- On/Off server
- Level Control / dimming
- physical PUSH control
- minimum brightness behavior
- power-on behavior
- reporting
- direct-device binding compatibility
- reliable electrical OFF
- OTA client if safely possible
- endpoint 11 unless evidence justifies changing it

Development builds must use an unambiguous identity such as `GL-SD-301P-ED`.

## Phase 1 rule: SOFTWARE-ONLY / READ-ONLY EVIDENCE

Before anyone opens the installed module or flashes anything, exhaust every practical software-only probe.

No:
- OTA update/downgrade/schedule
- custom image serving
- factory reset/re-pair
- binding mutation
- coordinator-wide changes
- security reset
- experimental writes to manufacturer-specific attributes
- opening the installed production unit

A separate supervisor comment gives the exact software-only acquisition procedure.

## Required decision after Phase 1

```text
MCU_EXACT =
POWER_STAGE_CONTROL = SECOND_MCU_UART / TELINK_DIRECT / UNKNOWN
OTA_IDENTITY =
FIRST_CUSTOM_OTA_FEASIBLE = yes/no/unproven
PUBLIC_STOCK_BINARY =
SOFTWARE_ONLY_BLOCKERS =
SPARE_REQUIRED = yes/no
```

If software evidence cannot prove the remaining hardware facts, stop cleanly and specify exactly what a sacrificial spare must provide. The production installed unit is not the first canary.

Migrated from analienx/bseed#9; this repository is the authoritative ledger for GL-SD-301P firmware work.
title: GL-SD-301P: non-routing RX-on-when-idle End Device firmware

> **Filed by triage 2026-09-04 on @danmt's ruling of the same day**, from an analysis of what a snapshot restore does to box-local engine state. The ruling is recorded in D1: *disable the weekly reset, keep the daily restart, and fold the reset back in on `0.1.4` — once durability is in, we can reset without fear.*

## Context
*(**Corrected in place by triage `2026-09-04`, hours after filing, on @danmt's report — and the correction is to the TENSE, not to the mechanism.** This body was written as though the weekly reset were running and the losses below were recurring. **They are not, and it was measurable rather than reported:** `shared/host-crontab.example` was created `2026-09-03` in [`7d14aff`](https://github.com/heavy-duty/crew/commit/7d14aff) and has exactly one commit in its history; #590 is an **unreleased** fragment in `changelog.d/`, absent from `CHANGELOG.md`, with `VERSION` at `0.1.3-dev`; and there is no installer for the host crontab. So the schedule has existed for one day, in an unreleased tree, and **has never been installed on any host**. @danmt confirms the fleet has run without a reset for roughly a month.*

*Three consequences, each carried into the text below rather than left here.* ***(i)*** *This issue is **prophylactic**: it stops the defect being introduced when `0.1.3` ships and an operator follows the runbook, rather than stopping an ongoing loss. That is a stronger position, not a weaker one — the fix lands before the schedule ever runs.* ***(ii)*** *The* ⚠️ *note in Dependencies asserted a weekly loss between now and this landing. **That is false in fact and is struck there.*** ***(iii)*** *`duty.log` therefore holds **far more than seven days** — nothing has truncated it — so the burn measurement this window wants is better-supplied than this body first claimed, and is under no Sunday deadline.*

***@danmt's acceptance, recorded because it is what makes the ordinary class right:*** *the fleet has worked a month without a reset, the disk risk in D5 is understood and accepted, `crew reset` stays available to run by hand if it is ever really needed, and the whole question **dissolves at `0.1.4`**, when the collector makes the evidence durable and the weekly job returns to the schedule as part of the flow.)*


[#590](https://github.com/heavy-duty/crew/issues/590) shipped `shared/host-crontab.example` with two job lines: `crew restart --all` daily at 04:10 and `crew reset --all` weekly on Sunday at 05:10. The weekly verb restores each roster box to its `armed` checkpoint — [`cli/crew:3484`](https://github.com/heavy-duty/crew/blob/main/cli/crew#L3484), `box restore "$name" "$RESET_LABEL" --force`. That is a **whole-VM snapshot restore with no carve-out for `$DUTY_DIR`** (`$HOME/duty`, [`shared/lib/common.sh:11`](https://github.com/heavy-duty/crew/blob/main/shared/lib/common.sh#L11)), so everything the engine wrote under it since the cut is gone every Sunday.

Most of what lives there is fine, and that was measured rather than assumed — the fix must not be sized as if the whole directory mattered:

- **Mentions survive.** Idempotency is GitHub-side, not ledger-side: `shared/prompts/mention.txt` marks each handled thread read with `PATCH /notifications/threads/<thread>` and says so — *"marking read is what makes this poll idempotent"*. A read thread is never re-delivered. `$DUTY_DIR/.seen-mentions` is only a **freshness filter** for the wake signal, so a restore costs at most one extra batched session, bounded by `MENTION_THREAD_CEILING=50`.
- **Declines survive.** `_decline_reason` reads the **board** — [`duty-builder.sh:111-124`](https://github.com/heavy-duty/crew/blob/main/shared/lib/duty-builder.sh#L111-L124), `gh api repos/$repo/issues/$num/comments`, own comments only, exact marker line. That is what #462 bought, and `.declined-build` is only the report ledger.
- **The `.seen-*` signal ledgers are cost-only and self-healing.** `build`, `review`, `ci-red`, `graph`, `unblockable`, `attention`, `discu
title: shared/host-crontab.example + docs/host-maintenance.md — the weekly reset restores the box and clears the resume breaker with no push, and takes duty.log with it

**Product, measured on production 2026-09-05 as a genuinely signed-out visitor**
(`document.cookie` empty, `localStorage` holding only `theme`).

A signed-out visitor who reaches `app.datanika.io/` waits **3.7 seconds** looking at a
painted but empty screen before anything readable appears. The three obvious
explanations are all wrong, and they have unrelated remedies, so this issue names the
one that is right.

## What it is not

| candidate | measurement | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Cold start / slow server** | document TTFB **318–337 ms**, consistent across `/`, `/login`, `/signup`, 3 samples each. `/healthz` 441 ms, `/ping` 490 ms | ruled out |
| **Redirect chain** | `performance.getEntriesByType('navigation').length` is **1**. `curl -L` reports `num_redirects=0`. The `/login` transition is a client-side route change | ruled out |
| **SPA boot / bundle size** | 2.25 MiB over 46 chunks, but **every asset completes by 837 ms**, cold. `loadEventEnd` 648–995 ms. Total long-task time 202 ms | ruled out |

## What it is

**A client-side route change gated on a backend round-trip — where the destination
route's JS chunk cannot even be requested until that round-trip returns.**

The controlled comparison, same browser, same session, same box:

| route | how reached | cache state | TTFB | load | **content painted (FCP/LCP)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/signup` | directly | **47/47 from network (cold)** | 337 ms | 995 ms | **800 ms** |
| `/login` | directly | 48/48 from cache (warm) | 318 ms | 420 ms | **444 ms** |
| `/` → `/login` | via `check_auth` | 46/53 from cache (warm) | 320 ms | 648 ms | **3656 ms** |

`/login` reached **directly**, warm, paints at **444 ms**. The *same page* reached
via `/` paints at **3656 ms**. The ~3.2 s delta is the redirect mechanism — not the
page, not the bundle, not the server. And note the `/` figure is the **warm-cache**
one; a first-time visitor pays the tail cold, which is where the ~6 s previously
reported comes from.

The waterfall names the mechanism:

```
   320 ms  document TTFB
   388 ms  first-paint          <- background only
   648 ms  loadEventEnd         <- SPA booted, all initial chunks done
   ...     2.6 SECONDS OF NOTHING
  3223 ms  GET /assets/_login_._index-BBuK70zD.js    <- first request for the login route
  3414 ms  ...arrives
  3656 ms  first-contentful-paint / LCP ("Datanika", the login card)
```

The client could not request `_login_._index-*.js` before 3223 ms because it did not
yet know it needed the login route. `/` is registered with `AuthState.check_auth` as
its `on_load`; that runs **in the backend**, over the websocket, after hydrate, and
returns `rx.redirect("/login")` (`auth_state.py:901`). Everything after is
serialized behind it.

**2.6 s is roughly 5x a round-trip on this box** (baseline above: ~450 ms end-to-end
including TLS, ~260 ms once connected). So the gap is not "one network hop" — most of
it is inside the hydrate/`on_load` path, and I did not narrow it further. Candidates
worth timing: websocket connect, Reflex's initial full-state serialization, and
`check_auth`'s own `await self.get_state(I18nState)` + `ensure_loaded()`.

## Why `/signup` and `/login` are fast, and why that is the fix

Neither page has an `on_load`. Their content is in the client bundle, so it paints
without asking the server anything — `/signup`'s FCP (800 ms) is **before** its own
`loadEventEnd` (995 ms). Only `/` has to ask.

## Scope — this is smaller than it was last week, deliberately

landing PR #513 pointed all 29 site CTAs at `/signup`, and that is live on `main`
(verified: homepage serves 6 `/signup` hrefs, 2 `/login`, 0 app-root). **So CTA
traffic no longer pays this at all** — it lands on an 800 ms page. What remains is
the residual population: someone typing `app.datanika.io`, a bookmark, or an old
external link.

That is why this is filed as a P2 and not as a launch blocker. It is also why it
should not be fixed by making `check_auth` route somewhere else — see cor
title: [Product] A signed-out visitor to / waits 3.7s on a blank screen — it is not cold start, not the bundle, and not a redirect chain

This is the place to discuss ideas before anyone opens a pull request, so that nobody builds something that will not be merged. Bugs belong in their own issue; this one collects what the app might do and what it deliberately will not.

Kept as an index. Every entry links to where it was discussed.

## Open

**Codes made of letters and digits, not only digits.** From the original post, and the one open half of it: the code length is configurable today, the character set is not. Small to build — the generator already reads the length from the settings, so it is one more setting plus the admin field, the `occ` key and validation, and the challenge input has to drop `inputmode="numeric"` when the set is not digits. Worth deciding first what it buys: six digits give a million combinations, six alphanumerics 2.2 billion, but guessing is already bounded by Nextcloud's brute-force protection on the challenge route and by the resend cooldown — while a mixed-case code is harder to type, harder to read aloud, and raises the question of ambiguous glyphs (0/O, 1/l). A longer numeric code may be the better answer to the same worry.

**A separate email address, used only for the second factor.** From the original post, marked "disputable" there, and it still is. Large: the app would have to store an address of its own, prove ownership before delivering to it (a verification round of its own), offer it in the personal settings and through `occ`, migrate existing accounts, and carry it in the code-to-address binding added in 3.5.0. It also changes what the app is — today Nextcloud owns and verifies the address, and the app only asks where to send.

The part that has no good answer is the administrator. An address that only counts once its owner has proved they read it cannot be set by anyone else, and that is not a detail: today an admin sets or corrects a delivery address with `occ user:setting`, and an LDAP or SAML backend can supply one that the user cannot change at all — which is exactly the "non-user-writable address from the directory" the original post above asked for. A verified app-owned address takes both away. The alternatives are worse than the feature: let the admin set it without verification, and the verification is decoration; refuse them, and provisioning a new account, fixing a typo, or moving a leaver's factor stops working. Before this is worth the weight, it needs a threat it answers that the account address does not.

## Declined

**Trusted device management**, [requested by @jonathan-ferme](https://github.com/datenschutz-individuell/twofactor_email/issues/8#issuecomment-4510247681): do not ask for a code on a device already known. It would mean this provider decides to skip the second factor, identifying the device by something the app itself hands out — an app-level bypass of the gate the app exists to hold. Nextcloud already keeps sessions alive across visits, and how long a session may live is a server setting. If a device-aware policy is wanted, it belongs in the server's authentication layer where every provider is bound by it, not in one provider.

**Enable email 2FA by default for new accounts**, and enforce it, [raised by @nc-enterprise-user](https://github.com/datenschutz-individuell/twofactor_email/issues/8#issuecomment-3238719127). Enforcement is a server setting and works today: with only one provider installed, every user has to set it up at first login. The remaining wish — switching the provider on before the user has ever logged in — saves two clicks and takes away the choice of another provider. The case where it would protect something turned out not to exist: [the walkthrough of both account-creation paths](https://github.com/datenschutz-individuell/twofactor_email/issues/8#issuecomment-3309996372), and [the follow-up](https://github.com/datenschutz-individuell/twofactor_email/issues/8#issuecomment-4338730084).

**HTML email.** [Ruled out](https://github.com/datenschutz-individuell/twofactor_email/iss

Jump to the last comment https://github.com/ramses-rf/ramses_cc/issues/1119#issuecomment-5546760792
Beginning of original discussion:

## Summary

`ramses_rf` as of 0.60.4 has a `PooledTransport` that aggregates multiple HGI transports (serial, MQTT, Zigbee) into a single logical transport with:

- Inbound deduplication (same packet heard by 2 HGIs → forwarded once)
- **Per-device RSSI** outbound routing (picks the HGI with the best
  signal for the specific target device, using `RssiTracker.best_rssi_for`
  — max of last N readings, consistent with PR 1123)
- **Source-ID re-patching** (frame's addr1 is re-patched to match the
  selected child's HGI before transmission — correct source ID per HGI)
- HGI filtering (accepted set — packets from foreign HGIs are dropped
  before dedup/forwarding, one set lookup overhead)
- Health monitoring (exclude silent/erroring children, re-enable as
  last resort)
- Graceful degradation (1 of N HGIs disconnects → pool keeps working)
- **Hot-reload** (add/remove children at runtime without restart)

The `pooled_transport_factory()` and hot-reload APIs in
`ramses_tx/transport/pooled.py` are ready to use, but `ramses_cc`
cannot configure or instantiate them yet.

## Goal: schema-driven pool membership

Pool membership is driven by the **schema**, not a hardcoded list of
port names. The schema already tracks HGIs (`18:...`) with `_class:
HGI` and `_owner`. We reuse this:

- HGI with `_owner: <root_owner>` → **included** in the pool
- HGI with `_owner: <other>` → **excluded** (foreign/neighbour's)
- HGI with `_disabled: true` → **excluded** (user disabled it)
- Unknown HGI (no `_owner`) → **discovery candidate** (accept/reject)

User flow:
1. User sets up the integration with one gateway (as today)
2. A second HGI appears on the RF network
3. The scan engine detects `18:` devices via its **raw packet handler**
   (registered with `add_raw_packet_handler`, fires before the device
   ID filter — see `protocol/base.py` line 727).  Unknown HGIs are
   allowed through the filter for eavesdropping (issue 822/1020), but
   the scan engine sees them regardless because it's a raw handler.
4. The user reviews the discovered HGI via the existing
   `review_discovered_devices` config flow step:
   - **Accept** → sets `_owner: <root_owner>` → HGI is added to the pool
   - **Reject** → sets `_owner: not-me` → HGI is blocked, not in pool
5. Later, the user can disable an HGI by setting `_disabled: true`
   (via schema edit or device health review) → HGI is removed from pool
6. If the user discovers an HGI is not theirs after all, they change
   `_owner` → HGI is removed from the pool

## How HGI IDs are discovered per transport type

### MQTT

**Single HGI (today, no pool)**: wildcard mode
(`mqtt://broker:1883/RAMSES/GATEWAY`). The transport subscribes to
`RAMSES/GATEWAY/+/rx`, auto-discovers the HGI ID from the first
packet's topic path, and locks onto it. Backward compatible, no
changes.

**Multi-HGI (pool)**: explicit children only, no wildcard. Each
accepted HGI gets its own child transport with an explicit topic:
```
Child 0: mqtt://broker:1883/RAMSES/GATEWAY/18:001234
  topic_pub = RAMSES/GATEWAY/18:001234/tx
  topic_sub = RAMSES/GATEWAY/18:001234/rx
Child 1: mqtt://broker:1883/RAMSES/GATEWAY/18:005678
  topic_pub = RAMSES/GATEWAY/18:005678/tx
  topic_sub = RAMSES/GATEWAY/18:005678/rx
```

The HGI IDs are known from the scan engine (which detects `18:`
devices from RF traffic via its raw packet handler). The coordinator
constructs the explicit MQTT URL and calls `pool.add_child()`.

**Multiple MQTT brokers**: supported. Each child is a separate
`MqttTransport` with its own connection. The pool doesn't care if
they connect to the same or different brokers. No need to prevent this.

**Why not wildcard for multi-HGI?** The wildcard child locks
`_topic_pub` to one HGI's `/tx` topic. It can only publish vi

## Authority
Single unattended controller for ZEL research-to-readiness progression. Immutable GitHub workflow artifacts are SSOT. No stage may advance without an explicit deterministic PASS receipt.

## Global locks
- Maximum one heavy VPS replay at a time.
- No duplicate strategy+axis+data-SHA replay.

- `selection_authority=false`, `promotion_authority=false`, `execution_authority=NONE`, `order_authority=BLOCKED` until the applicable later gate explicitly passes.

- [x] G2 Merge staged PR #565 into PR #562 head; accept Scalp artifact

## Research PASS gate
Every candidate must have exact source-owner and baseline trade/economic-digest parity; W1-only selection frozen through W2/W3; complete fee/slippage/funding lineage; errors=0; duplicate=0; censored-open=0; unknown-exit=0 where applicable; no future MFE/MAE leakage; no protected mutation. Economic survivor requires W1, W2, and W3 each: Net R>0, PF>=1, expectancy>0, payoff>=1, retention>=60%.

## Failure handling
Implementation/infrastructure defects: read-only diagnosis → one root cause → minimum patch → verify → at most two retries. Economic failure is recorded as terminal evidence and moves only to the next distinct approved causal axis; it is never treated as PASS. Secret/permission/quota/external-service blockers or the same cause failing twice force HOLD and user-authority request.

## User inspection
The controller must maintain one latest-state comment on this issue containing: stage, active PR/run/job, head SHA, artifact SHA, PASS/FAIL/HOLD, gate evidence, retry count, current blocker, next permitted action, and confirmation that Live/order authority is blocked. Ordinary in-progress updates need not notify the user; this issue remains the inspection surface.

> **PM spec pass (2026-08-31, rev 4 — GV-SIGNOFF received on rev 3; this rev folds the GV's two mechanical precision corrections, which it marked as needing no re-review).** The operator's original report is preserved verbatim below. The hypothesis section it carried has been **replaced** by the confirmed mechanism (the mem-admit token's dead-by-construction liveness proxy), and the ACs are restructured around it per the operator's suggested revision. The GV's four edits are all still bound; edit 1 lives in **#479** (Assumption A1). Two findings neither the operator nor the GV had are added below, both verified on `65afd84`: the `pgleader` link that makes the kill actually fire, and the fact that **#195 already solved this exact hazard in-tree** and the fix was never propagated to the library's read sites.

## What an operator hit

At 12:22–12:24 UTC on 2026-08-31, four gate runs were in flight concurrently (qa3 on PR #477, impl1 on #474, impl2 on #476, impl4 on #475). **Three of the four SIGKILLed a sibling role's *live* build tree**, and two of those produced `FAILED — SUITE` verdicts on PRs whose own suites had logged zero test failures.

| Killer | Log line | Reaped pgid | What that pgid actually was |
|---|---|---|---|
| qa3 | `gate-477.log:3255` | 3120395 | an older tree |
| impl4 | `gate468.log:3226` | 3800826 | **qa3's live gate run** |
| impl2 | `gate469.log:3226` | 3824594 | **impl4's live gate run** |

Each victim's log then carries the matching `<pgid> Killed` from `fwf-gate.sh:616` and a `fwf gate [#227 SUITE-level]: FAILED — SUITE`. The message emitted by the killer is `lib.sh:2257`:

```
fwf#156: reaping orphaned build tree (pgid $pgid) whose holder died — SIGKILL group
```

The holder had **not** died. It was another role's gate, mid-run.

## Why this is not a flake and not cosmetic

- The suite classifier labels the result `FLAKY: passed 9/20 recent runs` and reports `history (last 20 runs, ALL branches): 11/20 failed (last green 45m ago)`. A 55% failure rate spanning *all* branches is a property of the box, not of any diff.
- It is self-concealing. The classifier's `baseline: PASSES on merge base <sha> — this branch is the first place it is known to fail` reads as strong evidence against the branch under test, when the only real difference is how many gates happened to be running at the time.
- It cost real throughput: PR #477's *two* consecutive reds were both external kills, and the first was mis-attributed to the #119 lock-race flake in a PR comment, which sent qa3 into a pointless retry. A reviewer acting on these verdicts rejects good PRs; an implementer acting on them hunts a defect that does not exist.
- It scales with the thing we most want: parallelism. The factory runs four impls and four qas by design. The more of the floor is productive, the more often this fires.
- **Negative result that rules out the simple reading:** with three gates running concurrently and all confirmed alive after the burst, *no new cross-role kill occurred*. This is not "any two concurrent gates collide unconditionally" — it needs a specific contended step.

## Root cause — confirmed, `65afd84`

The GV's structural reasoning (a cross-role kill can only arrive through a **shared** reaper, because `fwf_gate_lock_dir` is role-keyed at `lib.sh:2691`) was correct and reached the answer ahead of the log evidence. The operator's grep then decided *which* shared reaper, and it is **neither** of the two originally suspected: not the e2e lane, not the cargo-build slot. It is the **mem-admit token**, and the consumer is the suite's own shellcheck step.

**Log confirmation.** All three harmful reaps sit at the identical suite position — the preceding line is `# shellcheck (if available)` (`test/run.sh:12624`), the sole site acquiring the shared token. impl1's benign startup reap is a different lock, and its own log says so:

```
fwf: ANOMALY — reaping gate lock for 'impl1' (held by dead pid 3797450)
fwf#156: reaping orphaned build tree
title: Concurrent gate runs SIGKILL each other's live build trees: the fwf#156 reaper declares a live sibling's holder dead, and the kill is reported as FAILED — SUITE

## Purpose
Central coordination point for concurrent TornHappyGymStats fleet work. This is **not implementation backlog and not an agent-task lease**. Actual default branch is `main`.

## Absolute authority boundary
Fleet/manual agents may create, update, review, merge and consolidate work only on **NON-DEFAULT** branches. They must **never merge any branch or PR into `main`**. Final default review/merge belongs exclusively to Gerome's coding-agent/human workflow.

## Claim protocol — two phase
Before overlapping mutation, refresh this issue body + recent comments, target issue/PR, current `main`, target/stable head; post one concrete `🔒 CLAIM` with lane, unique `run=<token>`, exact issue/PR/branch/package/seam and head SHA where practical; immediately reread recent comments. Earlier GitHub comment ID wins overlaps; later claimant releases its own claim and chooses independent work. Two failed acquisitions => back off. Release the same claim when work stops.

#140 coordinates ownership only. Never write `lease: #140` into `hgs-evidence`; ordinary work without a real #62 lease uses `lease: none`.

## Head CAS

## Summary

Codex Security is missing the final, operationally critical stage of the security lifecycle: **responsible disclosure**.

Codex can increasingly help a researcher discover, validate, reproduce, write up, deduplicate, and track security findings. The current Codex Security tracking workflow can route validated findings into project-management or source-control destinations such as GitHub issues/security advisories and other trackers. But when the finding is a vulnerability in OpenAI itself—or another vendor with a coordinated disclosure / bounty program—the researcher still has to leave Codex, manually reconstruct the report in a separate system, re-establish program scope, move evidence, submit it, and then manually maintain the linkage between the Codex finding and the disclosure case.

That is a major missing architectural layer.

For OpenAI specifically, the gap is especially conspicuous because OpenAI's coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy asks researchers to report vulnerabilities, bugs, safety/abuse issues, and security flaws; the Security Bug Bounty uses Bugcrowd for submission/reward management; and the Safety Bug Bounty is a separate program that may reroute reports with the Security team depending on scope.

Codex Security should therefore support **first-class disclosure providers and a tracked submission lifecycle**, rather than ending at an internal tracking ticket.

## Related existing issues

This proposal is part of the same broader reporting/intake architecture discussed in:

- #32225 — identifies a private security/engineering feedback-intake failure for sensitive Codex incidents and asks for selective evidence submission, stable case IDs, and confirmation that reports reach the correct team.
- #37583 — proposes an OpenAI-native, trackable issue/reporting system instead of fragmented `/feedback`, support, GitHub, Community/Discord, etc.
- #37585 — proposes recognizing substantial verified bug-reporting work because producing high-quality reports consumes real user time and paid Codex capacity.

Those issues cover important pieces of the same system. This issue focuses on the missing **security-disclosure branch**: once Codex Security has a validated finding, it should be able to carry that finding through authorized responsible disclosure and track the resulting case.

## Current failure mode

The present workflow is effectively:

```text
find
  -> validate
  -> reproduce
  -> write up
  -> classify
  -> package evidence
  -> track internally
  -> STOP
```

The human researcher must then manually perform:

```text
find the right disclosure program
  -> re-check scope
  -> authenticate to the external program
  -> copy/reformat the report
  -> re-attach evidence
  -> submit
  -> capture report ID
  -> monitor triage
  -> respond to information requests
  -> track duplicate/accepted/rejected/payout state
```

This is precisely where a security workflow should become *more* structured, not less.

## Proposed architecture

Add a first-class **Responsible Disclosure** stage to Codex Security:

```text
finding
  -> validated
  -> disclosure_candidate
  -> program_fit
  -> evidence_sealed
  -> submission_previewed
  -> user_approved
  -> submitted
  -> tracking_id
  -> triaged
  -> accepted | duplicate | rejected | needs_information
  -> fixed / disclosed / payout / resolved
```

The system should distinguish at least three destination classes:

1. **Internal tracking**
   - GitHub issue
   - GitHub security advisory
   - other internal trackers

2. **OpenAI responsible disclosure**
   - OpenAI Security Bug Bounty (currently Bugcrowd-backed)
   - OpenAI Safety Bug Bounty
   - appropriate OpenAI security incident / coordinated-disclosure route when a bounty program is not the correct destination

3. **Third-party responsible disclosure**
   - provider interface for Bugcrowd / HackerOne / vendor-native portals / security.txt or documented vendor intake
   - bounded by the target's published policy a
title: [Codex Security] Add first-class responsible-disclosure and bug-bounty submission/tracking

## Summary

In a long-running, tool-heavy Codex Desktop agent thread, automatic context compaction reports success (`Context automatically compacted`) but the context meter immediately remains at roughly **80% full**. This leaves only about 20% usable runway before another compaction cycle.

The result is a repeat loop:

`compact -> resume nearly full -> run a few tool operations -> compact again`

This is not merely a cosmetic meter problem. The affected thread repeatedly reprocesses state, loses working coherence, spends substantial paid usage, and becomes unreliable for production repository work.

## Environment

- Product: Codex Desktop
- Platform: Windows 11
- Subscription: ChatGPT Pro
- Workload: long-running agentic repository coordination with many tool calls, GitHub operations, command outputs, and image evidence
- Observed: July 23, 2026
- A public elevated-error-rate incident was active at the time. This is included for correlation only; causality is not established.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use a Codex Desktop thread for a long-running repository task with repeated tool calls and large tool outputs.
2. Continue until automatic context compaction occurs.
3. Observe the visible `Context automatically compacted` event.
4. Immediately inspect the thread's context-usage indicator.
5. The thread remains approximately 80% full directly after compaction.
6. Continue for a small number of operations; compaction triggers again.

## Observed behavior

- Successful compaction reclaims only about 20% of the context window.
- Multiple compaction events occur close together.
- The active thread retains or rehydrates too much prior tool/output history.
- The agent repeats plans, loses acceptance criteria, and contradicts earlier state.
- Paid usage is consumed during repeated compaction/reprocessing without proportional task progress.
- The user can reach the usage limit while the production task remains incomplete.

## Expected behavior

- A successful compaction should produce substantial working headroom, not resume near the next compaction threshold.
- Replacement history should be bounded, deduplicated, and exclude raw historical tool output that is no longer needed in the active prompt.
- If compaction cannot reclaim enough space, Codex should explicitly report compaction failure or recommend a bounded handoff to a new thread rather than silently continuing near capacity.
- Context telemetry should distinguish original history, compacted summary, retained tool state, and reserved output space so this can be diagnosed.

## Impact

This blocks reliable long-running agent work and creates direct usage waste. A production coordination thread became trapped in repeated compaction while repository progress stalled.

The reporter has screenshots showing the compaction events and the thread remaining about 80% full immediately afterward. Private repository names and paths are intentionally omitted from this public report.

## Related reports

- #24948 — repeated compaction history and raw tool output cause huge session logs
- #34971 — massive cached context is repeatedly reprocessed, causing latency and excessive credit use
- #19585 — unusually fast usage depletion worsened by unstable context compaction
- #21134 — long active Codex Desktop threads remain unusable despite transcript pruning
- #29967 — auto-compaction occurs at the threshold and needs stronger pre-turn handling

This issue is narrower: **the visible auto-compaction completes but immediately leaves the active thread around 80% full.**
title: Codex Desktop auto-compaction completes but leaves long-running thread ~80% full, causing repeat compaction and usage waste

**Severity: Medium — silently wrong GPU stats on a fairly common hardware configuration**

### Issue type

- [x] Bug - something is broken or not working correctly

### What happened?

On my Ryzen APU + discrete AMD GPU desktop, the GPU usage widget shows roughly half of what either GPU is actually doing under load — running a game that pegs the discrete card at 100% while the iGPU sits idle at 0% displays as ~50% in the bar/Nexus resource widgets.

Root cause: `shell/plugin/src/Caelestia/Services/gpu.cpp`, `readGenericUsage()`:
```cpp
const QStringList paths = QDir("/sys/class/drm").entryList({"card*"}, QDir::Dirs | QDir::NoDotAndDotDot);
qreal sum = 0.0; int count = 0;
for (const QString& card : paths) {
    QFile f(QString("/sys/class/drm/%1/device/gpu_busy_percent").arg(card));
    if (f.open(...)) { sum += f.readAll().trimmed().toDouble(&ok); ++count; }
}
const qreal newPerc = count > 0 ? sum / count / 100.0 : 0.0;
```
This walks *every* `cardN` entry that exposes `gpu_busy_percent` and averages them into one number with no attempt to identify which card is the "real"/active GPU (discrete vs integrated, or primary vs secondary in a multi-GPU box). The type-detection script a few lines up (`kTypeDetectScript`) already treats "any card with `gpu_busy_percent`" as sufficient to classify the system as `GENERIC`, so this isn't a one-GPU-assumption edge case — it's the intended code path for any non-Nvidia system, and it breaks the moment there's more than one DRM card. The temperature path has the identical problem: `readGpuTemperature()` calls `sensorslib::gpuPciAverageTemp()` — the function name says it all.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On a system with an AMD iGPU and AMD/other dGPU both exposing `gpu_busy_percent` under `/sys/class/drm/card*/device/` (common on Ryzen "G"/APU desktops paired with a discrete card, and some AMD Advantage laptops).
2. Load only the discrete GPU (e.g. run a game forced onto it) while the iGPU stays idle.
3. Compare `cat /sys/class/drm/card1/device/gpu_busy_percent` (the loaded card) against Caelestia's GPU usage widget — the widget reads roughly half the real value because it's averaged with the idle card's 0-2%.

### Caelestia version

main branch

### Distro

Arch (Ryzen APU + discrete AMD GPU)

### Logs or screenshots

`for f in /sys/class/drm/card*/device/gpu_busy_percent; do echo "$f: $(cat $f)"; done` next to the widget's displayed percentage shows the widget consistently landing at the arithmetic mean of the per-card values, not the max or the active card's own value.

---
_Note: this is a different code path from #314 (`detectTypeOnce()` misclassifying hybrid Nvidia+other systems as pure Nvidia) — that one is about GPU-type detection; this one is the `GENERIC`-path usage/temperature math itself, which averages across cards regardless of which type won detection. Possibly related to the in-progress #588 ("Redo gpu.cpp"), which doesn't currently mention this specific averaging behavior — flagging here in case it isn't already covered by that rewrite._
title: GPU usage and temperature are averaged across every /sys/class/drm/card* device, producing meaningless numbers on hybrid-graphics/multi-GPU systems

Status: **PLANNED — CURRENT INV-002 HARD-FAILURE PROPAGATION / IMPLEMENTATION WIP=0 / REVIEW WIP=0**

## Discovery

Read-only audit of current `main@8346477f6f6f2fd814f759cd0f6d1f192ce10947` finds that INV-002's deliberately separate rollback-invariant failure state is not preserved consistently through gameplay service wrappers.

Accepted #209 states that if a real commit unexpectedly fails and exact checkpoint restoration also fails, that outcome is surfaced separately as a **HARD TRANSACTION ROLLBACK INVARIANT FAILURE**, never as an ordinary clean rejection.

Current `InventoryTransactionService._rollback_after_commit_failure(...)` returns the failed transaction result with:

```gdscript
success = false
rollback_restored = false
```

plus diagnostics prefixed with:

```text
HARD TRANSACTION ROLLBACK INVARIANT FAILURE
```

This matters because `rollback_restored=false` means the transaction service could not prove exact canonical participant restoration after mutation began. Callers must not collapse that into the same semantic class as a preflight/capacity/material rejection where canonical state is known unchanged.

## Current preservation matrix

### Correct: EquipmentService

`EquipmentService.equip_from_inventory()` / `unequip_to_inventory()` return the raw failed InventoryTransactionService result when commit fails.

Therefore `rollback_restored` survives.

### Correct: LootRewardService

Loot collection wraps the raw failed transaction result inside its failure data and does not consume PendingLoot after failed commit.

Therefore the lower transaction result remains mechanically inspectable.

### Defect: CraftingService

`CraftingService.craft()` currently projects the transaction result into a new Dictionary containing only:

```text
success
recipe_id
diagnostics
transaction_fingerprint
operation_count
events
plan_descriptor
```

It does **not** carry `rollback_restored` or a stable equivalent hard-failure discriminator.

Thus an INV-002 rollback-invariant failure becomes indistinguishable to downstream code from an ordinary failed craft except by parsing developer diagnostic strings.

### Defect: ProgressionCraftEquipService

The accepted craft/equip progression bridge further maps failures through `_failure(...)` / `_equip_failure(...)` using only diagnostics and selected fingerprints/events.

Consequences:
- a CraftingService hard rollback failure is already lost before progression receives it;
- an EquipmentService result that correctly contains `rollback_restored=false` is stripped when `equip_existing()` maps it into a progression failure;
- higher production composition cannot mechanically distinguish a clean craft/equip rejection from a transaction whose exact rollback failed.

This affects the accepted mounted weapon progression path as well as future #417 composition if left unresolved.

### Coordination: SurfaceHarvestInventoryService

`commit_yield()` correctly returns the raw failed transaction result.

`rollback_yield()` currently converts a failed inverse rollback transaction into its local `_failure(diagnostics)` shape, dropping any `rollback_restored` value while appending a textual `HARD INVARIANT` diagnostic.

#585 already owns replacing that inverse-operation compensation with exact canonical restoration. This card must **coordinate**, not duplicate #585: whatever final #585 rollback mechanism uses, an inability to prove exact restorat

## Status
Architectural refactor proposal. **No gameplay/balance change is intended by this issue.**

## Problem
`runtime/js/dicebound.js` has grown into a very large monolithic runtime bundle (currently roughly 15k lines / 1.3 MB). It owns many unrelated responsibilities in one file: game bootstrap, state, board flow, combat, classes, items/loot, powerups, pets, progression, rendering/UI glue, events, mode logic and various compatibility patches.

This makes otherwise-small changes risky because:
- unrelated systems are physically coupled in one huge file;
- ownership of functions/state is difficult to see;
- later definitions/patch blocks can silently override earlier behavior;
- reviewing a change requires navigating a massive source file;
- testing individual systems in isolation is difficult;
- multiple contributors/agents touching the same file creates unnecessary merge conflicts;
- future save/resume, balancing and content work becomes harder than it needs to be.

The existing `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` already identifies `dicebound.js` as the recovered monolithic game bundle and explicitly recommends incremental, behavior-preserving extraction into explicit modules. This issue makes that direction a concrete project.

## Goal
Move DiceBound toward a structure familiar from component-/object-oriented development:

- a **small bootstrap/main entry point** that starts the game and wires major systems together;
- each major gameplay/domain responsibility owned by a smaller module;
- clear public interfaces between modules rather than unrelated functions reaching into each other's internals;
- explicit state ownership and dependency direction;
- substantially reduce `runtime/js/dicebound.js` until it is either a small compatibility/bootstrap file or can be removed entirely.

This does **not** mean every concept needs to become a JavaScript class. Use classes where stateful objects genuinely benefit from them, and plain modules/functions/data registries where those are clearer. The important goal is separation of responsibilities and explicit ownership.

## Architectural principles

1. **Incremental extraction, not a rewrite.**
   - Move one coherent subsystem at a time.
   - Keep the game runnable after every extraction PR.
   - Prefer mechanical moves first; redesign only after behavior is preserved.

2. **Behavior preservation is mandatory.**
   - No intentional balance, loot-rate, class, combat or progression changes as part of this architectural issue.
   - Unexpected behavior differences are regressions, not refactor side effects to accept casually.

3. **Keep browser + native compatibility.**
   - The same `runtime/` must continue to work in direct Edge/browser launch and inside the native WebView2 wrapper.
   - Do not require Node/npm or a developer toolchain on the player's machine.
   - Browser-native ES modules are acceptable if verified in all supported runtime paths; otherwise use explicit deterministic module loading/namespaces.

4. **Make dependencies explicit.**
   - Avoid hidden reliance on ambient globals where practical.
   - Avoid circular module dependencies.
   - Prefer modules receiving state/services they need over reading arbitrary unrelated globals.

5. **One authoritative owner per function/system.**
   - Remove the current pattern where later patch blocks can redefine an earlier function and silently become the real implementation.
   - When a subsystem is extracted, its final runtime implementation should live in one clear place.

6. **Preserve save compatibility.**
   - Moving code between files must not silently alter the persistent save schema.
   - Save/resume work is tracked separately; coordinate with it rather than coupling an unrelated save-format redesign into this refactor.

7. **Keep historical release evidence immutable.**
   - Do not rewrite `docs/releases/beta-0.6/` to match the new source layout.

## Suggested target layout
This is a starting point, not a rigid final tree:

Read-only audit of current `main@8346477f6f6f2fd814f759cd0f6d1f192ce10947` plus accepted #209/#217/#431 contracts finds a persistence safety gap after a **hard canonical rollback failure**.

INV-002 explicitly distinguishes an unexpected commit failure whose exact checkpoint restoration succeeds from one whose restoration cannot be proven:

```text
success = false
rollback_restored = false
```

#209 calls the latter a **HARD TRANSACTION ROLLBACK INVARIANT FAILURE**. #640 now owns preserving that machine-readable evidence through Crafting, Progression, Loot, Surface acquisition and Resource composition, including Resource cases where WorldDelta exact restoration also cannot be proven.

However current `Game.build_save_request()` has no runtime-trust/quarantine input. It validates ordinary snapshot prerequisites such as:
- exact root/session state;
- valid WorldDeltaStore object;
- live/non-defeated Player;
- Inventory/Equipment type and codec compatibility;
- pending-loot reconstruction;
- finite resume/vitals.

It then captures the current Inventory/Equipment/WorldDelta as durable truth.

A rollback failure is different from malformed structure: the partially restored participant may remain **structurally valid** and may still pass `validate_container()`, MAP encoding and the current gameplay codecs. Therefore current SAVE can potentially persist a state that the runtime has explicitly failed to prove equivalent to either the pre-operation or intended committed result.

That would turn a process-local hard invariant failure into a durable canonical save and make the next Continue treat an untrusted intermediate state as legitimate history.

Neither #217 nor #431 owns this post-runtime-failure trust state. #640 explicitly stops at preserving/propagating the evidence and does not design SAVE policy.

## Core invariant

> **Once a gameplay operation reports that exact restoration of a canonical participant cannot be proven, the current Game session must not serialize those participants as trustworthy durable SAVE state unless a later explicit recovery operation re-establishes canonical trust.**

For V1, the smallest safe policy is a **latched SAVE-ineligible runtime trust state** for the current Game session.

- Inventory transaction `rollback_restored == false`;

- invalid preflight;
- transaction commit failure followed by verified exact rollback (`rollback_restored == true`).

`#20` is closed and correctly so: the template placeholder is gone and the enclave now runs Helico's own re-centre decision. But the prize wording asks for more than a real decision — it asks that the workflow be *"a meaningful part of the application"* and rules out *"an isolated example that does not contribute"*.

Today the verdict is computed and then goes nowhere. Nothing on-chain consumes it. An assessor reading the repo would be right to call that isolated.

## What closes the gap

The standard CRE delivery path, verified on both sides while reviewing #34 and #36:

1. The vault implements `IReceiver` and an `onReport(bytes metadata, bytes report)` that only the `KeystoneForwarder` may call.
2. `report` is exactly the bytes the enclave emits with `encoderName: 'evm'`, so the vault does `abi.decode(report, (bool act, int24 tickLower, int24 tickUpper, bytes32 mandateHash))`, requires `mandateHash == keccak256(abi.encode(m))` for the account it is acting on, and then runs the existing `recenter` logic.
3. `AGENT_ROLE` moves from an EOA to the forwarder, so the only thing that can propose an action is a decision that came out of the enclave.
4. On the workflow side it is one call: `EVMClient.writeReport(don, { receiver: vault, report, gasConfig })`.

That is what makes the confidential workflow load-bearing rather than adjacent: with it, no re-centre can happen that the enclave did not decide.

## The constraint that shapes it

A `KeystoneForwarder 1.0.0` is deployed on **Robinhood Chain Testnet** at `0x8E6E6A1f2B2D4dF503bfd67951CF28F27BF3AF19`; the same address has **no code on Robinhood mainnet**, and mainnet is not in Chainlink's forwarder directory (verified on-chain by @rifkyeasy on #33).

So the DON-delivered path is demonstrable on the testnet today. Doing it on mainnet would mean our own relayer carrying DON signatures — which is exactly the shape of thing the twelve-agent audit just showed is hard to make safe, and not something to build in the last week.

**This decides which chain the demo video runs on**, so it should be settled before #22 rather than during recording.

## The shape that is not yet decided

`recenter` takes `RecenterParams`: `owner`, the two ticks, `liquidityToMint`, four slippage bounds and a deadline. The report carries four of those. The rest has to come from somewhere — widened report, on-chain derivation, or mandate fields — and that choice interacts with the missing `liquidityToMint` floor recorded in #34.

## Done when

- [ ] The vault accepts a verdict from the forwarder and rejects one from anywhere else, with a test for each
- [ ] `AGENT_ROLE` is held by the forwarder in the deployed configuration, not by an EOA
- [ ] A re-centre on Robinhood Chain Testnet, triggered by the workflow, with the transaction hash recorded for #21
- [ ] The package README stops saying the vault does not consume the report
title: Deliver the enclave's verdict to the vault through the CRE forwarder

## Purpose

**Single running log for everything discovered mid-implementation that must not derail the ticket in flight.**

While working any ticket, if you hit a bug, a missing piece, a wrong assumption, a pitfall, an
external constraint, or a scope gap — **do not fix it inline and do not silently drop it.** Append
it here as a comment and carry on with the ticket you are on.

Use `/backlog "<note>"` to append. Every entry must state where it was found so it is traceable.

## Entry format

```
### <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM> · found in <TICKET-ID> · <type>
**What:**        one line
**Impact:**      what breaks or is at risk
**Workaround:**  what we did instead (or "none — deferred")
**Action:**      fix now / fix Day 4 / accept as limitation / document in HLD
```

`<type>` ∈ `bug` · `gap` · `pitfall` · `constraint` · `assumption-wrong` · `perf` · `security` · `data-quality`

## Triage rule

- **Blocks the current ticket's AC** → fix now, and still log it here.
- **Breaks a later ticket** → log, and add a `blocker` note as a comment on that ticket.
- **Neither** → log and defer. Do not touch it.

## End-of-project use

Before submission this ticket is read in full and split into three lists:
1. **Fixed** — closed inline, referenced by commit
2. **Accepted limitations** → these go verbatim into the deck's *"What this system does not do"* slide

## 🎉 Add`Smart Heading` Recognition Feature For Word Document

Starting from v1.5.5, LightRAG's built-in DOCX parser introduces the **Smart Heading** feature -- enabling better section-based chunking even for poorly formatted DOCX documents.

Many DOCX documents have visually clear section structures but lack properly configured Word outline levels, or retain incorrect heading styles from editing, copying, and concatenation processes. In the past, these issues could cause section titles to be treated as body text, or regular text to be misidentified as headings, resulting in chunking boundaries that deviate from the document's true semantic sections. For P chunking strategies that rely on heading structures, this creates fragmented context or mixed content from different sections, affecting subsequent indexing and retrieval.

**Smart Heading** targets such poorly formatted but semantically clear documents, restoring their true heading structures as much as possible:

1. **Recover Missing Section Titles**: Identify content that visually appears as titles but lacks properly configured outline levels, reducing loss of section structures.
2. **Reduce False Positives of Body Text as Headings**: Restore regular body text, complete clauses, captions, dates, and version notes that incorrectly carry heading styles back to body text, avoiding meaningless chunking boundaries.
3. **Improve Inconsistent Heading Hierarchies**: Reduce issues such as inconsistent sibling heading levels, inverted parent-child hierarchies, and skipped levels, making section structures more coherent.
4. **Distinguish Multiple Contents in Merged Documents**: Identify main titles and document boundaries of each piece of content, preventing section level interference between different documents.
5. **Reduce Noise from Long Tables of Contents**: Compress excessively long table of contents, minimizing the interference of duplicate information on indexing and retrieval.

By providing more reliable section structures for subsequent chunking, Smart Heading helps maintain semantic associations between titles and their corresponding body text, making chunking results align better with the document's original content organization.

**Summary**

`deploy/reference/README.md`'s "Operating notes from a real cluster" section credits the Goobernetes spike and carries the storage-role split, the taint contract, the CSI mode-bit rule and the `subPath` trap. Ten further facts were measured on the same cluster over the following three weeks, each cost a real incident, and none is written down anywhere upstream. All are substrate-neutral; all are one to three sentences.

**The ten notes (each with the Infra ledger row that paid for it)**

1. **Pin the remote base by the full 40-character SHA.** A short SHA renders locally and fails `git fetch` inside kustomize's remote-base checkout. (M-06)
2. **Give the remote base a fetch budget** — `?ref=<sha>&timeout=<seconds>` — because kustomize's default 27 s checkout aborts under load and the failure reads as a render error. (I-108)
3. **A worker seeded with `instance.yaml` alone starts healthy and fails its first stage.** The worker needs the config *tree*; the symptom is fail-late, not fail-fast. (M-07; upstream #3314/#3290 track the product half)
4. **The input to the pod grace-period formula is the longest single-stage ceiling, not the longest duration in the config** (a branch drains at a stage boundary), and **per-attempt ceilings live in two places** — `GooberSpec.TimeoutSeconds` and task-level `timeoutSeconds` — so a workflow-file-only audit gets the number wrong silently. (M-09, M-11)
5. **On AKS a pod grace period over 30 minutes is inert unless the node pool's drain timeout exceeds it**; the drain timeout must move with the grace period. (M-08)
6. **A CSI `SecretProviderClass` is all-or-nothing: one unresolvable entry 404s the whole mount** and takes every other secret in that class with it. Use one class per blast-radius domain. (I-25 / L-157)
7. **For a static PV binding, `storageClassName: ""` and an omitted `storageClassName` mean different things**; omitting it lets the default class dynamically provision a fresh empty disk beside the durable one. (`patches/pvc-static-binding.yaml`)
8. **On AKS with Windows nodes, Calico is the only NetworkPolicy engine left** (Cilium is Linux-only; Azure NPM's Windows support retires 2026-09-30), and Calico on AKS is CIDR-only, so FQDN allowlists need a forward proxy. (L-01/L-02)
9. **When both namespaces default-deny, both halves of a flow need a policy, and the symptom of the missing half is a timeout, not a 401 or an x509 error.** (`egress/blob-ingress.yaml`, `egress/worker-daemon-ingress.yaml`)
10. **The config-tree ConfigMap transport has a ~1 MiB ceiling**; state it as a limit rather than let it be discovered. (I-03, #3290)

**Impact**

Each of these is a first-week incident for a stranger, and the reference README is the only place they would look. Nine of the ten are three sentences or fewer.

**Acceptance criteria**

- [ ] The ten notes land in `deploy/reference/README.md` §"Operating notes from a real cluster", each with its mechanism (why), not just the rule.
- [ ] Notes 1–2 also appear as comments in the remote-base example overlay from #4283.
- [ ] `make ci` green (the README is not generated, so no drift guard fires; this is a prose change).

**Blast radius / risk**

Documentation only. Parent: #2909 (the guide these would eventually fold into).

Part of #264. Discovered while connecting real #270 release admission to managed onboarding.

## Objective

Implement the accepted PRD's explicit Preview opt-in through the normal managed Elsa onboarding and durable lifecycle path, without relabeling a producer preview as Supported or weakening default eligibility.

## Verified gap

On source `22c531bd`, admission defaults catalog entries to Preview. Managed onboarding, create eligibility, and the durable resolution input source only allow Supported; the create contract has no preview consent. The workspace catalog lifecycle query is read-only and does not grant eligibility. The current behavior safely denies Preview but does not implement the [PRD's explicit opt-in requirement](https://github.com/valence-works/elsa-control/blob/22c531bd7964f3a2e2247b70e7fefcde91fed65e/docs/product/elsa-commercial-platform-prd.md#L136).

## Scope and constraints

- Add explicit, authorized consent bound to the selected managed-instance release and workspace/actor boundary. Persist the consent so worker resolution after restart can verify the same immutable release authority.
- Keep default behavior Supported-only. Merely listing Preview catalog entries, caller-supplied lifecycle strings, or a global admission configuration change must not grant consent.
- Align onboarding options, request validation, durable worker resolution, and the console's clear Preview warning/confirmation.
- Preserve API intent/outbox commit followed by asynchronous worker resolution; retain idempotency, strong preconditions, reservation/CAS, and safe audit semantics.
- Preserve arbitrary release/version cardinality. Do not introduce version-number branches or silently promote producer/catalog lifecycle.
- Do not make Maintenance or End of Support eligible for new instances through this opt-in.

## Acceptance

- [x] No-consent requests and old clients remain denied for Preview.
- [ ] An authorized customer explicitly opts into one eligible immutable Preview release and creates the instance through the public product path.
- [x] Durable consent survives fresh-context reload; changed/ambiguous release identity, stale consent, cross-workspace and unauthorized requests fail closed in automated contracts. Live public worker acceptance remains part of the unchecked product-path gate.
- [x] Supported onboarding remains unchanged; Maintenance/End of Support remain blocked for creation.
- [x] Console warning and explicit consent are browser-tested against an isolated fixture API; API/resolver/persistence/security tests cover the same gate.
- [x] No raw manifests, secrets, provider payloads or arbitrary diagnostic text enter consent/audit records.

## Dependencies / readiness

Builds on delivered #270 and #265 and the existing governed catalog. Implementation is in PR #276; public rollout remains gated on the separate SQL bootstrap cleanup fix #277 and catalog migration rehearsal. Root and independent reviews cover the implementation, console, migrations and contract. This is a product-path gap, not a defect in #270 signature verification and not evidence that #264 is complete.

## Reviewed implementation contract

- Add optional `PreviewManifestDigest` to `ElsaReleaseIntent`. A supplied value requires an explicit requested version and canonical lowercase `sha256:<64 hex>` syntax. Consent is per exact intent/release selection, not a mutable workspace-wide grant. Existing authorized actor/intent audit records the authorization.
- Persist the nullable field on both current instance and intent-revision entities, including mappings and SQLite/SQL Server migrations. Consent must survive a fresh context/restart.
- Add the canonical release JSON entry only when non-null. Null must preserve existing canonical JSON bytes and hashes; a consent-only change must still produce a distinct desired-state revision/idempotency identity.
- Null keeps Supported-only selection. Non-null selects the exact paid distribution/line/version/channel/topolog

## Goal

Let users select newly released conversational text models from their AI provider without per-model approval, paid qualification, or an application-maintained model allowlist. Prefer native web search, make external search credentials optional, and continue with reduced capabilities when optional features are unavailable.

## Agreed behavior

- The provider model listing determines model availability. Known embedding/image-only endpoints are outside feed generation; unknown capability metadata must not exclude a conversational model.
- Model and capability discovery performs only free listing/metadata requests. Never run inference, web search, or compatibility probes as part of background synchronization.
- Refresh credential-specific availability separately from credential validation. Refresh daily, when opening a stale picker, and on explicit refresh. Preserve the last successful snapshot during transient failures and keep credentials usable during refresh.
- Enrich provider metadata with free published metadata where appropriate. Missing capabilities and prices remain unknown, rather than becoming unsupported or free. Do not treat metadata from a different provider/endpoint as proof of identical behavior.
- Keep the selected model stable. A temporary listing omission must not silently substitute a different model.
- Native search is the default for new feeds. Preserve explicitly selected external search credentials on existing feeds. External selection is an override; if retrieval is unavailable, use remaining capabilities and record the limitation.
- Search and page fetching are independent. A supplied URL can be fetched by the application and passed to a model without function calling.
- Missing optional features must not prevent model selection, preview, or feed enablement. Losing an optional search credential must not automatically disable its feeds.
- Adapt prompts to the actual tools/content available. Allow useful responses from supplied content or general knowledge, but do not turn a limitation explanation into a publishable post or present invented current source updates as retrieved facts.
- Keep local output validation mandatory. Invalid output may fail an individual run cleanly without marking the whole model unsupported.
- Capability fallback handles specific unsupported-feature errors with a bounded number of attempts. Authentication, rate limits, outages, malformed application requests, and arbitrary integration defects need distinct handling.
- All attempts share a run budget and preserve usage accounting, including provider-native search. Never report unknown prices as zero.
- No permanent supported/unsupported certification for individual models. Retain targeted live probes as optional development diagnostics.

## Implementation sequence

1. **Minimal execution path**
   - Make text-only execution work without tools or API-enforced structured output.
   - Request JSON through instructions and validate locally; allow a bounded repair attempt.
   - Separate gathering and structuring when their combination is unsupported.
   - Keep provider API/transport differences inside the existing client/adapters; avoid a general compatibility framework.
   - Establish this path before removing the existing qualification gate.

2. **Automatic discovery and open selection**
   - Remove `LlmModelCapability` and qualification-dependent selection after the minimal path is established.
   - Add non-disruptive, free synchronization with supported/unsupported/unknown capability metadata.
   - Ensure models missing from the SDK's bundled registry can still be invoked through their provider using exact model IDs.
   - Preserve account isolation, selected models, and the last successful catalog.

3. **Optional retrieval**
   - Integrate actual provider-native search, including the appropriate endpoint/SDK transport.
   - Implement external search override and fallback to supplied URL content or no web access.
   - Update

Part of #548 and #899. Blocks the fresh replacement challenge required by #1085. The source-level safety and suitability work remains separately owned by #903 and #1086.

## Why

The v5 holdout is burned diagnostic evidence. Its immutable replacement lineage excludes every original source, all 36 rendered request videos, all selected anchor families, and every programme-parent provenance.

A deterministic audit of the frozen authorities proves the current inventory cannot produce a replacement:

- programme parents: 0 unexposed against 6 required;
- bumper anchors: 1 otherwise eligible and unexposed against 2 required;
- PSA anchors: 0 against 2 required;
- trailer anchors: 2 against 3 required;
- promo anchors: 2 against 2 required;
- commercial anchors: 9 against 3 required.

Those are raw role counts only. Duplicate-family, source, duration, transition-band, transition-stratum, same-role/cross-role pair, media-quality, and suitability constraints can reject additional candidates.

## Outcome

Acquire, condition, measure, and truth-lock a source-diverse replacement pool that can satisfy holdout-plan v4 without any prior source/request hash, family, or programme-provenance leakage.

Target a buffer rather than the mathematical minimum:

- at least 10 eligible programme parents from 10 distinct provenance records, so 6 can survive selection;
- at least 4 newly eligible bumpers;
- at least 6 newly eligible PSAs;
- at least 4 newly eligible trailers;
- at least 2 additional promos and 2 additional commercials when they add underrepresented transition strata.

The hard floor remains 6 programme parents, 1 bumper, 2 PSAs, and 1 trailer. The buffered target exists because a pool that merely meets counts can still fail the joint transition solver.

## Source rules

- Prefer primary, rights-traceable audiovisual collections with stable item metadata and direct media bytes.
- Bind licence or public-domain basis, item URL, retrieval time, exact source bytes, and immutable metadata bytes.
- One item URL or edition is one provenance parent; mirrors and alternate encodes do not create independent truth.
- Reject material already present in any v5 source or rendered request by exact hash and perceptual duplicate family.
- Do not use Met Open Access images as programme-video substitutes. They may support later visual interstitial controls, but they do not satisfy this moving-image corpus gap.
- Keep source acquisition separate from truth, safety, and production admission.

## AI-first review

This must not become another blind full-corpus human labeling exercise.

1. Run deterministic rights, decode, audio/video coverage, duration, duplicate-family, and transition measurements first.
2. Use local ASR/OCR/vision plus bounded multimodal models to propose unit, role, boundaries, and hazard observations.
3. Reject obvious non-candidates mechanically.
4. Show the maintainer only surviving candidates, prefilled with evidence and model disagreements.
5. Require complete audiovisual playback only for the small set proposed as truth anchors or disputed at decisive boundaries.
6. Model agreement nominates evidence; it never becomes truth authority by vote.

## Gates

1. A pre-download search manifest states desired role, source authority, item identity, rights basis, and expected media before bytes are fetched.
2. Every downloaded candidate has a content-addressed ledger and complete decode/coverage measurement.
3. Exact-byte and duplicate-family checks run against the full v5 exposure set before review.
4. The accepted pool meets the buffered targets or documents why the joint solver succeeds with less.

### What happened?

Found this driving a real checkout form with a tokenized-card iframe from a third-party PCI-compliant payment provider, cross-origin from the app's own page. `page.frames()`, `page.frame({url})`, `page.frame({name})`, `page.frameLocator(...).locator(...)`, and `page.mainFrame().childFrames()` all fail to find or interact with the iframe's content — Playwright behaves as if the iframe doesn't exist.

I want to be precise about why I think this is worth reporting, and not just an unavoidable security restriction: in a real Chrome + Playwright session, CDP is specifically designed to grant an attached debugging client access into cross-origin iframes for exactly this kind of testing — that's how real e2e suites drive tokenized payment iframes (Stripe-style and similar) today. It is not blocked by same-origin policy for a CDP client; that's the point of the protocol.

I dug further before concluding anything, and found something more precise than "not reported at all":

- A direct `Page.getFrameTree` call (via `page.context().newCDPSession(page)`) shows the bridge's response **does** correctly include all 3 cross-origin child frames present on the page, each with the right `id`, `url`, `securityOrigin`, and `parentId` (see log below). So the data genuinely exists on the bridge side.
- But `Page.frameAttached` **never fires** for them — zero occurrences across a full `DEBUG=pw:protocol` trace, including through a live `page.reload()` that recreates the iframes fresh.
- Playwright's frame-manager appears to build its internal Frame objects only from live `Page.frameAttached`/`Page.frameNavigated` events, not by walking `getFrameTree`'s `childFrames` array on the initial snapshot. So even though the bridge has the correct data, Playwright never learns these frames exist, and every frame-lookup API comes back empty.

For contrast: a **same-origin** child frame (an `about:srcdoc` frame) *did* get a `Page.frameNavigated` event correctly in an earlier trace this session, so the bridge's live frame-event translation works for at least some child frames — just apparently not these cross-origin ones.

**Went one level lower to rule out any Playwright-side misunderstanding on my part**, since I wanted to be sure before reporting this: bypassed Playwright's Frame abstraction entirely and called `Page.createIsolatedWorld` directly via `page.context().newCDPSession(page)`, explicitly passing each of the three distinct, confirmed-real `frameId`s from the frame tree (`0.38`, `0.42`, `0.46` in this session — a `CardNumber` field frame, a `Cvv` field frame, and an `Emv3ds` frame respectively). **Every single one of the three returned an execution context bound to the same wrong frame** — a Cardinal Commerce device-fingerprinting sub-resource nested three levels deep inside the `Emv3ds` frame (`frameId 0.50`), regardless of which of the three top-level frameIds I actually requested. Confirmed via `document.URL` inside each returned context — always the same fingerprinting URL, never the frame I asked for.

So this isn't just "Playwright doesn't learn about these frames" — the bridge's own `Page.createIsolatedWorld`, when given an explicit, correct, verified-real `frameId` for a cross-origin child frame, doesn't actually scope the resulting execution context to that frame. It seems to always resolve to some other frame (possibly the most-recently-created one, or a fixed internal one) regardless of the `frameId` parameter. That would explain both symptoms at once: Playwright never gets a live `frameAttached` for these frames (so it can't build a Frame object), *and* even a raw, explicit CDP request to target one of them directly doesn't land where requested.

If my read is right, this would block any tool from ever correctly reaching this kind of content — not fixable by DOM/Input domain work alone, since even direct, low-level frame targeting doesn't work yet for cross-origin children specifically.

### How can we reproduce this?
title: webinspector cdp: cross-origin child frames unreachable — Page.frameAttached never fires, and Page.createIsolatedWorld with an explicit frameId resolves to the wrong frame
