Part of #17. Phase 1 of the delivery plan ([`docs/delivery-plan.md`](../blob/main/docs/delivery-plan.md)), scoped for a single builder. This is the full Phase 1 gate, not one layer of it.

## Problem Statement

Pulse today is documentation plus an empty skeleton. Nobody can create an account, no Medical History can be held for anyone, and none of the platform's promises can be shown to an examiner. A person cannot register, prove their email address, sign in, or look at a Patient's profile in their own language. There is also nothing stopping a future API route from silently returning data to whoever calls it.

## Solution

A working skeleton a person can actually use:

- A visitor registers with an email, a password and a Role. A verification email lands in Mailpit; clicking the link activates the account.
- They sign in and receive a session cookie that expires on idle and has a hard cap. Signing out ends the session; "sign out everywhere" ends all of them.
- Changing credentials asks the person to re-enter their password (step-up).
- A signed-in Patient lands on their own seeded Patient profile, rendered in English or Hindi, with a working locale switch.
- Behind the screens: every API route declares who may call it, and CI fails a route that declares nothing. The conventions that make consent enforceable later — every clinical read composes from one query builder, modules never import each other — are wired now, while there are three routes and not sixty.
- `git clone && docker compose up` on a machine that has never seen the project produces this working, seeded, sign-in-able system.

## User Stories

**Registration and identity**

1. As a visitor, I want to register with email, password and a chosen Role, so that I get a User account.
2. As a visitor, I want my password stored with Argon2id (via `pwdlib[argon2]` at library defaults), so that a database leak does not expose it.
3. As a visitor, I want invalid registration input rejected with field-level error details, so that the form can highlight the offending inputs.
4. As a visitor, I want registering with an already-registered email to fail with a stable `EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED` code, so that the frontend can show a "sign in instead" path.
5. As a newly registered person, I want a verification email to arrive in Mailpit, so that I can confirm my address for the demo.
6. As a newly registered person, I want to complete verification by following the emailed link, so that my account becomes fully usable.
7. As a person who lost the email, I want to request a fresh verification challenge, so that a delivery failure is recoverable.
8. As the system, I want verification challenges to carry a TTL, so that a leaked old email cannot be redeemed later.
9. As an unverified person, I want to be able to sign in but be blocked from any permissioned action with `EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED` until I verify, so that the frontend can render a "resend verification" screen from a signed-in state.
10. As the system, I want verification to run through `IdentityProvider.start_verification` / `complete_verification`, so that ABHA's two round-trip flow drops in later without touching services.

**Login and session**

11. As a registered, verified person, I want to sign in with email and password and receive an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` session cookie, so that subsequent requests are authenticated.
12. As a user, I want my session stored in Redis under `sha256(token)`, never the raw token, so that a Redis dump yields no usable sessions (ADR-0003).
13. As a user, I want a sliding 60-minute idle lifetime, so that continued activity keeps me signed in.
14. As a user, I want an absolute 12-hour cap on any session, so that a stolen cookie cannot live indefinitely.
15. As a user, I want wrong credentials to fail with one generic `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` code with no distinction between "no such email" and "wrong password", so that my email is not enumerable at the login endpoint.

A sub-author who optimises the number can reach it by deleting comments and move no ownership at all. That is why the band is an acceptance *signal* and the Ownership test is the *gate*; the measurement is recorded here so the distinction cannot be lost downstream.

The defect is not size. It is that the file holds behaviour **whose destination already exists**. `window/TearOut.mjs` has been present and imported for months while the tear-out cluster stayed behind — the lead datum that falsified Option D in the source Discussion, offered by its own author.

This needs an Epic rather than a ticket because the concerns do not share one lifecycle, one optionality profile, or one landing order: some are pure classification, one is declinable stateful presentation, one cannot move until the sibling lane's Group exists, and the façade contract can only be written after the owners it fronts do.

## Intended solution shape

**Option G — a vehicle per responsibility; `Workspace` becomes a façade, not the vehicle.** Emmy's Step-Back names G as governing. The classification, offered in the Discussion to be falsified and not falsified since:

- model classification / document transformation → pure `model/*`
- a two-method holder capability a named external consumer resolves → a narrow mixin is admissible (`window/TopologySeams.mjs` is the passing precedent: one `className` config, no state, exactly the two methods `DockService` resolves)
- an optional concern with state and teardown → a plugin or owned collaborator
- cross-concern ordering and the one mutation boundary → the `Workspace` façade

**If the same concern appears in two rows, the split is wrong.**

### Target anatomy

The v13.2 **folders** were right and stay; what changes is which files exist inside them and what `Workspace` no longer holds. One new folder, on in-package precedent (`src/tab/plugin/Overflow.mjs`, plus five modules in `src/plugin/`):

```
src/dashboard/dock/
├── Workspace.mjs                 façade: ordering + the one mutation boundary
├── plugin/                       NEW — declinable, stateful, engine-owned teardown
│   └── Maximize.mjs              maximize + FLIP motion (observer + transition lifecycle)
├── projection/
│   └── HeaderActionPolicy.mjs    NEW — the action-policy cluster (membership stays in
│                                 toolbar.Base#getActionItems / tab.header.Toolbar#isTabButton)
├── window/
│   ├── TearOut.mjs               EXISTS, under-used — receives the pane-handle choreography
│   └── WorkspaceSet.mjs          folds into the participant side of the Group seam
└── model/                        unchanged: pure classification already lives here
```

Two clusters are load-bearing and measured. **Header-action policy:** of 21 methods / 853 LOC, 12 methods / 609 LOC read workspace-only sta

FlowBalance: Verifier-Grounded Self-Improvement from On-Policy Reasoning Experience
Abstract
FlowBalance improves reasoning models via verifier-calibrated self-guidance using trajectory-level score reweighting and profile-based trajectory balance.
A reasoning model can improve from its own on-policy experience, but this inner loop is fragile: terminal verifiers provide reliable yet sparse supervision, while dense same-model guidance can reinforce false confidence or overconcentrate learning on a narrow solution mode. We introduce FlowBalance, a verifier-grounded self-improvement method that learns a normalized distribution over complete responses. For each on-policy trajectory, a frozen training-time view of the same policy uses privileged context to produce token-level log-probability gains, which are aggregated into a trajectory-level self-guidance score. FlowBalance calibrates this score with the verifier-derived group advantage: guidance is retained on positive-advantage trajectories, reversed on negative-advantage trajectories, and disabled when the rollout group provides no outcome preference. The resulting energy exponentially reweights a reference policy, and profiled trajectory balance fits the normalized target with one log-partition estimate per rollout group. This realizes outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance, without a separate token-level imitation loss. Our analysis establishes within-group contrast preservation, a minimum-change reverse-KL characterization, monotonic verifier control of target reward, and an exact correction against false-positive self-guidance on rejected responses. On mathematical reasoning, FlowBalance improves average performance over FlowRL on both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, while also improving training speed and stability, avoiding direct OPSD's response-length collapse, and exhibiting higher correct-strategy diversity in a controlled AIME24 diagnostic.
Community
FlowBalance is a verifier-grounded self-improvement method for reasoning models. It addresses one known failure mode of OPSD on thinking models: privileged feedback can reinforce locally plausible but verifier-wrong traces. FlowBalance combines sparse outcome rewards with dense self-feedback while flipping misleading teacher support on failures.

body_excerpt:
Helico is already a chat. The dapp's whole front door is a sentence turned into a
checked intent, and the only reason it lives in a browser is that a browser is
where a wallet is. Telegram is the same interface without the browser — and it is
the only surface we have that can *start a conversation*, which is the thing a web
page fundamentally cannot do.

This is a design for review, not a plan of record. @ghozzza — the three decisions
I would most like you to disagree with are marked.

## The constraint that shapes everything

**A Telegram bot cannot sign, and must never be able to.**

Every safety argument in `contracts/` rests on the same two facts: the owner's
wallet signs, and the agent's reach is the owner's allowlist. A bot that could
move money would be a bot that holds a key, and one compromised bot token would
then reach every account that ever talked to it. `HelicoAccount._requireOwnerOrAgent`
admits `owner()` or the nominated `agent` and nobody else; a Telegram process is
neither and must stay neither.

So the question is not "how does the bot swap for you". It is **what is worth
doing that needs no key at all** — and the answer turns out to be most of it.

## Three tiers, in the order they are worth building

**1. Read — needs no key, no signature, no new trust.**

> `/portfolio` → 1,240.00 USDC · 840.00 working in Aave
> `/mandates` → 2 live · 1inch SwapVM · 4,000 USDC still spendable
> `/moves` → 3 movements today, last at 14:02

Every one of these is already answerable: balances from the chain, mandates and
movements from our subgraph. This is where the Graph work pays for itself twice —
the cache from #213 means a hundred `/portfolio` messages cost one Studio query a
minute rather than a hundred.

**2. Notify — the reason to be on Telegram rather than on a page.**

> The agent moved 800 USDC into Aave. Your mandate has 3,200 USDC left.
> A venue you revoked has been unwound. Nothing is left there.
> This mandate is 90% spent.

A web app cannot tell you this while the tab is closed. This is the tier that
makes the bot worth having and it is also the one that needs the most care about
what we are willing to promise.

**3. Compose, but never sign.**

> "put half my idle USDC to work"
> → I read that as: supply 620 USDC to Aave v3 on Arbitrum One.
> → [Open in Helico to sign] ← a deep link

The bot runs the sentence through the intent endpoint `apps/be` already has,
shows what it understood, and hands back a link that opens the dapp with the
intent prefilled. **The signature happens exactly where it happens today.** The
bot's output is a suggestion and a URL.

## Linking a Telegram account to a wallet

A Telegram chat is not authentication. The bind must be proven by a signature, and
we already have the verifier for it — `apps/be/internal/session` checks an EIP-712
payload against a nonce it issued.

```
/link
  ↳ bot:  open https://app.helico.site/link?code=7f3a…  (valid 5 minutes)
  ↳ user: connects the wallet they already use, signs the same payload the
          session flow signs, with `code` as the nonce
  ↳ be:   verifies, binds telegram_user_id ↔ wallet, one row in the SQLite we have
  ↳ bot:  Linked to 0xa29e…fcd4. /unlink at any time.
```

No new cryptography, no new key material, and `/unlink` is one message. A bind
proves *the wallet consented to this chat* and nothing else — it grants no
authority over the account, because there is no authority to grant.

## Where the code goes

`packages/plugins/telegram`, as `@helico/plugin-telegram`. Per CLAUDE.md, apps
never talk to a protocol directly — the Bot API client, update parsing and message
formatting live in the package; `apps/be` consumes it and owns the routes and the
database.

```
packages/plugins/telegram/     the Bot API: send, edit, answer, parse an update
apps/be/internal/telegram/     the handlers — what a command means, what it reads
apps/be  POST /api/telegram/webhook
```

**Webhook, not long polling.** The VPS already terminates TLS and Cooli
title: Helico on Telegram: a design to argue with before any of it is written

body_excerpt:
The plan is for Helico to do what a wallet's agent should be able to do — swap, lend and borrow,
stake, earn, hold a perp, pay for its own inference, bridge, and compose those into one
transaction — across chains, starting with two. This is the design for that, written before any
of it is built.

**This is not work for the 13th.** Six days out, the submission is one thing proven: a mandate the
vault enforces and an enclave that decides. Everything below is the shape it grows into, and the
one part of it worth pulling forward is argued at the end.

---

## 1. The chain choice: Arbitrum One and Base

Between Base, Arbitrum and Ethereum, the two are **Arbitrum and Base**, and Ethereum is the one
left out on purpose.

**Ethereum is wrong for this product, not too small for it.** The whole premise is an agent that
acts repeatedly under a mandate — re-centring a range, rolling a position, topping up a payment
channel. Each of those is a transaction, and on mainnet each one costs enough that the mandate's
economics invert: the agent spends more defending the position than the position earns. Helico's
`minImprovementBps` exists precisely to refuse moves that are not worth their cost, and on
mainnet that guard would refuse almost everything. The place mainnet wins — native LSTs, the
deepest lending — is the place we care least.

**Arbitrum** is where we already are, and where perps actually live (GMX v2). **Base** is where
x402 lives — 119M transactions — and where Morpho is bigger than Aave. Uniswap v4 is deployed on
both, and both appear in the Graph Explorer with a v4 subgraph:

```
Arbitrum   D1VHPU6cXXSC8eaApWCjCnPcTZQFSYCpGoDAvt4ogDWh
Base       2L6yxqUZ7dT6GWoTy9qxNBkf9kEk65me3XPMvbGsmJUZ
```

**Corrected after review (#142 comment):** those ids came from the Explorer, not from a
reproducible check. The obvious `curl` against `gateway.thegraph.com` returns an identical
`auth error: missing authorization header` for a **fabricated** id, so it distinguishes nothing.
Published-and-indexed is therefore still unverified by anything anyone can repeat without a key,
and section 7's risk 1 is larger than it says.

---

## 2. The change everything else depends on

Today a mandate is one struct:

```
rangeWidthTicks · minImprovementBps · cooldownSeconds · maxLiquidity · minRetainedBps · expiry
```

That is a mandate for **one job**. `maxLiquidity` means nothing to a perp. `minImprovementBps`
means nothing to a payment. And the limit that matters most for lending — *never let the health
factor fall below X* — has nowhere to live in it.

So the first change is not a protocol integration. It is this:

> **A mandate becomes a set of typed capability grants, not one struct.**

```
Mandate {
  expiry
  grants: [
    { capability: LP_RECENTRE, params: { rangeWidthTicks, minImprovementBps, minRetainedBps, maxLiquidity } },
    { capability: SWAP,        params: { allowedTokens, maxNotionalPerDay, maxSlippageBps } },
    { capability: LEND,        params: { market, minHealthFactor, maxBorrowed } },
    { capability: PAY,         params: { maxPerDay, allowedRecipients } },
  ]
}
```

Two properties to keep from what we have, because they are the reason the vault is trustworthy:

- **The vault reverts anything outside the grant.** It never rewrites an action to fit — it
  refuses it. The consequence is worth stating in the README, because we already have it and never
  say so: a grant can only ever narrow what the agent may do, so a mistake in a grant costs the
  owner an action, never their funds.
- **Revocation needs nobody.** `revoke()` works while the contract is paused, while the agent is
  gone, and while an upgrade is pending. That must survive the generalisation — one call kills
  every grant, not one grant at a time.

---

## 3. Structure — and there is more here already than I expected

```
                        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   person ──sentence──▶ │  apps/app        chat, gate, mandate UI  │
title: Beyond one capability: the multi-protocol design, two chains, and where The Graph carries weight

This is not a request to add a specific feature. Rather, I would like to share a research implementation that may be of interest to the Grid2Op community and to ask for your technical feedback.

Hello Grid2Op development team,
First of all, thank you for developing and maintaining Grid2Op. It has proven to be an excellent research platform for studying decision-making algorithms in power systems and for performing objective comparisons between different control approaches.
Over the past several weeks, we have been investigating a new online control strategy based on a structural representation of the power system state.
Instead of reinforcement learning, the controller continuously evaluates two characteristics of the current network state:
- external nonequilibrium of the system (ΔN);
- internal structural heterogeneity (ΔD).
These quantities are then used by the "Combinatorial Compression Engine (CCE)" to select control actions through a limited number of predictive simulations.
The current implementation combines three physical control channels:
- energy storage control;
- generator redispatch;
- network topology control using "set_bus" actions.
All candidate actions are evaluated using a common structural risk metric and participate in the same online decision-making process.
During local testing on the official deterministic "l2rpn_idf_2023" scenario (fixed seed), we obtained the following results:
- "Do Nothing baseline:" grid collapse after 9 steps;
- "DN / CCE controller:" successful completion of the entire scenario (300/300 steps).
The controller evaluates approximately 32 candidate actions per decision step and operates entirely online, without reinforcement learning, offline training, or precomputed action databases.
Unfortunately, the official CodaBench submission phase had already closed by the time this work was completed, so we were unable to evaluate the controller through the competition infrastructure.
Nevertheless, we have published the complete implementation and would greatly appreciate your technical feedback on the proposed approach.
Project repository: https://github.com/Zhenis-ref/DN-Controller-Grid2Op
We would be particularly interested in your opinion regarding:
- the proposed online decision-making algorithm;
- the structural state representation used by the controller;
- the possibility of evaluating this approach on additional Grid2Op scenarios or benchmarks.
If you have an opportunity to evaluate the controller using your own testing infrastructure or additional Grid2Op environments, we would greatly appreciate your independent assessment. Since the official competition has already concluded, an evaluation by the Grid2Op development team would be especially valuable. We would welcome any feedback, whether positive or critical, that could help us further improve the approach.
Thank you once again for your time and for developing such a valuable platform for the research community.
Best regards,
Zhengis Tileubay
Independent Researcher
Kazakhstan
title: Proposal of a New Online Controller for Grid2Op Based on Structural State Dynamics (DN / CCE)

## Passing

| Item | Evidence |

| At most three partner prizes | two: Uniswap Foundation and Chainlink |
| Demo video script | `docs/demo-video-script.md`, 3:30, inside the window |

## The one thing worth deciding

**Eleven merges on `main` are squashed**, so eleven pull requests appear as one commit each rather than as the work that produced them: #67 (19 commits), #70, #72, #75, #77 (4), #84 (10), #98 (7), #102 (2), and three more. That is 11 of 215 commits, and the rest of the history is proper merges.

The rule this touches is the one with teeth: judges inspect commit history, and *"you cannot just have three commits with a million lines"* is a finalist-track disqualification. We are nowhere near that shape — 215 commits, 63 merges, small and frequent — but #67 and #84 in particular each hide double figures of real commits.

**The work is not lost.** Every head branch still exists and every original commit is fetchable from `refs/pull/N/head`, which is how I checked. A judge reading `git log` on `main` will not see them, and a judge reading the pull requests will.

Squash and rebase merging are **off** in the repository settings now, so this cannot grow. Three options, and this is Ghoza's call:

1. **Leave it.** The pull requests carry the detail, the history is otherwise clean, and eleven commits out of 215 is not the failure mode the rule describes.
2. **Restore the eleven**, by reverting each squash and re-merging its branch with a merge commit. No history is rewritten; `main` gains the real commits and eleven reverts. It is honest but noisy, and the noise is itself something a judge reads.
3. **Say it in the README** — one sentence pointing at the pull requests for the fine-grained history of those eleven.

I lean to 3, and would do 2 only if Ghoza wants the history to stand alone without the pull requests.

- **Nothing is deployed to a live network.** `apps/cre/workflow/config.production.json` still has the zero address for the vault. ### **Description:**

In 2026, agentic memory has a dirty secret: **your agent's memories are trapped.** Every memory platform stores your agent's accumulated knowledge — learned preferences, resolved contradictions, hard-won context — in its own proprietary schema. Switch tools, and it all evaporates. Your agent starts over with amnesia.

We believe agentic memory should belong to *you*. That's why Memanto ships with a full migration and portability toolchain, built on the **[Open Knowledge Format (OKF)](https://docs.memanto.ai/integrations/okf)** — Google Cloud's open, vendor-neutral spec for knowledge as plain markdown. With Memanto today you can already:

- **Migrate in** from Mem0, Letta, or Supermemory with a single command: [`memanto migrate`](https://docs.memanto.ai/cli/migrate/migrate) — complete with dry-run previews and token/latency/storage savings reports
- **Export out** to a portable, git-friendly, human-readable OKF bundle: `memanto memory export --okf`
- **Import any OKF bundle** losslessly: `memanto migrate okf ./bundle` — unmapped fields are preserved, nothing is lost
- **Sync** a browsable memory wiki into any project: `memanto memory sync --okf`

The tools exist. What the world hasn't seen yet is the **movement**. We want the open-source community to show every agent builder — vividly, virally, with real data — what it looks like to *escape lock-in and own your memory*.

Build a **compelling, reproducible migration showcase** that takes memories from another tool into Memanto and out again as portable OKF — proving the full freedom loop: **in → owned → portable**.

⚠️ **Do NOT reinvent the wheel.** The `memanto migrate` CLI and OKF export/import are shipped and documented. Your job is to build *on top of* them — real-world showcases, new migration paths for tools we don't support yet, and creative OKF workflows. Submissions that re-implement what the CLI already does will score poorly on engineering value.

`Requested-by: exec:ceo` — CEO RUN 23, claim `ceo-2026-09-04T12:20:48Z`. The remedy half of **#1597**; that issue holds the analysis and stays open for the standing question.

## The headline, and it is not the licensing question

The public-adjusting analysis came back **clean on the product** — no Otter Quotes surface constitutes public adjusting, because we do not participate in determining what the carrier pays, which is the element that matters in every one of the three regimes. Full analysis: `Stellar Edge Services/Otter Quotes/Legal/public-adjusting-analysis-2026-09-04.md` (22,610 B).

**What it found instead is worse in the near term and cheaper to fix: two of our own published statements are false as sent.** Neither is a licensing problem. Both are truthfulness problems on the claim path, and one of them is in an email that goes to a third-party insurance adjuster over our domain.

### 1 · The disclaimer is falsified by a live feature

`guides/how-to-file-property-damage-claim.html:633` publishes that Otter Quotes **"does not handle communications with your insurer."**

`supabase/functions/send-adjuster-email/` sends email to the homeowner's adjuster **from `Otter Quotes <noreply@…>`**, written in the homeowner's voice.

Those cannot both be true. We are telling homeowners we stay out of the insurer conversation while operating a feature whose entire purpose is to enter it. **Fix the disclaimer to track the statutory verbs — what we do not do is participate in determining what the carrier pays, advise on settlement adequacy, or negotiate — rather than making an operational promise the product breaks.** Replacement wording is in the analysis.

### 2 · `send-adjuster-email/index.ts:239` — the Reply-To contradicts the body

The email body tells the adjuster that a reply **"will come straight to me"** (the homeowner). The `Reply-To` header points at **our ingest address.**

**This is untrue as sent, and it is untrue to a third party in an insurance matter, independent of any licensing question.** It is also the single fact most likely to make an otherwise-clean analysis read badly to a regulator, because it looks like an intermediary quietly inserting itself into the carrier channel while telling both sides it has not.

**Fix: set `Reply-To` to the homeowner.** If there is a product reason we want the reply (threading, the claim timeline), then change the *body* to say so plainly — "replies come to Otter Quotes and appear in your claim timeline" — and keep the header. **What is not available is the current pair.**

### 3 · Five `on your behalf` strings

Including a UI that literally renders **"Otter Quotes (on behalf of you)"**. "On behalf of" is the operative phrase in the definitional sections of all three statutes. It costs nothing to say something else and it removes the phrase a regulator's keyword search finds first.

**⛔ EXCLUSION LIST — do not sweep these:** `privacy.html:406` (CCPA statutory language, must stay verbatim) and the auto-bid strings (a different, accurate use). A blind find-and-replace here creates a compliance defect while fixing a cosmetic one.

### 4 · Two guides carry no boundary disclaimer at all

`guides/how-to-negotiate-with-insurer.html` and `blog/how-to-negotiate-better-roof-repair-insurance-claim.html`. **The house boundary box already exists elsewhere in the corpus** — paste it. Note these two are the most exposed pages we publish, because Indiana's IC 27-1-27-1 reaches *"advice or assistance in the adjustment"* with no negotiate/settle limiter and **no contractor carve-out**, and both pages are titled as negotiation advice.

### 5 · Constrain the unbuilt call script to document requests only

Cheapest control point on the board: one sentence about estimate adequacy would land the script inside IC 27-1-27-1. Constrain it before it is written, not after.

## Why this is `must` and not a copy-tidy

R-156 bar (a): **legal exposure**, and a live false statement to a third party in an insurance

Add Seafile as the platform's sixteenth service: file sync and share, converged by Ansible like every other stack, with its verification, monitoring, upgrade and recovery story wired in from the first commit rather than retrofitted.

`docs/adding-a-service.md` is the how, and it is authoritative — read it rather than this issue for the mechanics. What follows is what is *specific to Seafile*, plus the cross-cutting work that is easy to omit because no single test names it until much later.

## Why Seafile is not a normal service here

Three properties make this harder than the last fifteen, and each one shapes the work below.

**It is multi-container with a database.** Four containers: the server, MariaDB, Valkey and Elasticsearch. Only `immich` and `paperless-ngx` have that shape today — everything else is a single container — so those two are the precedent to copy, including how they name and order their containers and how their roles wait for the database before touching the application.

**Its primary artifact is the user's own files.** Not metadata about media that could be re-fetched: the documents themselves. That puts its data squarely in `recovery: critical` and makes the backup section below the most important part of this issue rather than a footnote.

**Files on disk are not the files.** Seafile stores content as content-addressed blocks under `seafile-data/storage`, with the mapping from blocks to filenames living in the database. A filesystem backup taken without a consistent database dump restores an unreadable pile of blocks. This is the single most important thing to get right, and nothing in the existing platform's backup story has had to handle it.

## Edition: Pro, decided

Seafile PE is free for up to three users and needs **no license file** at that size. Since v12.0 the Pro images are on Docker Hub and need no registry authentication — earlier versions were behind `docker.seadrive.org` with Customer Center credentials, and some of Seafile's own pages still describe that flow, so confirm with an unauthenticated `docker pull` before building around it. The current tag at time of writing is `seafileltd/seafile-pro-mc:14.0.6-testing`; pick a stable tag, not `-testing`.

This resolves the auditing question below: Pro has a real audit log, so that section is a requirement rather than a hope.

Two things this decision costs, neither fatal:

- **The three-user cap is a hard ceiling**, counted on activated accounts. Above it, Pro is a paid subscription. Worth being sure three is genuinely enough before building around it, because the alternative at user four is either paying or migrating to CE and losing the audit log this edition was chosen for.
- **A missing or unreadable license degrades to "trailer mode", capped at three users.** At this size that is indistinguishable from normal operation, so there is no cliff to monitor — noted only so nobody later reads the phrase in a log and treats it as an incident.

## Stack decided

**MariaDB.** Forced rather than preferred: Seafile has no Postgres backend. Both existing multi-container stacks here run Postgres (`immich_postgres`, `paperless_postgres`), so this is the platform's **first MariaDB** and it inherits none of their backup verb, upgrade constraints or pinning pattern. A new database engine to own, not a reuse.

**Valkey for the cache**, not Memcached and not stock Redis. Seafile 13 makes the Redis protocol the recommended path and leaves Memcached as legacy; `immich` and `paperless-ngx` already run `docker.io/valkey/valkey:9`, so matching them keeps one cache image across three stacks — less for Renovate to track and one fewer distinct pull per CI matrix. **Verify Seafile accepts Valkey** rather than assuming: it is a drop-in for the protocol, but a server-version string check would surface immediately.

**Elasticsearch, for full-text search.** This is a sync-and-share service standing in for Google Drive, where search over content — not filenames — is the f

## Theme Name

Intent-based security policies: expression, coexistence, and runtime verification

## Proposer(s)

Cyril Gorlla (CTGT). Builds on candidate theme 2 from the 29 July preparation meeting; co-development welcome, particularly from the IETF and access-control side.

Appraisal checks and starter vector set (AVS-0.1, 2 September 2026) contributed into task 3 by @tyche-dev, Tyche Institute, under his name.

## Summary

Classical access control binds rights to a verified identity, but a verified identity says little about how an agent will behave on a given task, and revoking an identity does not reliably stop unwanted behavior. Deployment adds a sharper version of the problem: an agent that passes every identity and authorization check can still produce an output that violates the very policy it was authorized under. This theme explores expressing security policy as intent, properties that must hold regardless of which actor is involved, and extends the July 29 scope with a third question: how a relying party verifies, at the moment of action, that an agent's behavior conforms to the intent, and what verdict that verification produces. Discussion on #1 and #5 has refined when a requirement binds, and what question a theme answers. On the first, the requirements are concurrent, since recording, provenance, and evaluation all bind at or before the moment of action. On the second, the questions retain an order, since a party cannot reconstruct an act that has not occurred. #5 specifies the reference; this theme specifies the evaluation of an action against it; #1 specifies the record. Of the three, this is the only one specifying a decision rather than an artifact, which is where interoperability bites: two implementations can agree on a provenance format and a record format and still disagree on whether a given action conformed.

## Scope / Open Questions

Three tasks. Tasks 1 and 2 are from the original theme; task 3 is the proposed extension.

**Task 1, expression.** How can a security policy be expressed as an intent, independent of the actors and agents involved? Features and limits, including the semantic-delegation risk raised on July 29 (Xiaoya Yang): a properly authenticated, authorized delegation can still be interpreted differently than the delegator intended. The hard case #5 raises borders this task and splits in two: whether a natural-language goal constitutes a grant of authority at all is prior and belongs to #5, since by the time an evaluator sees anything a grant has been assumed; how conformance is tested against an imprecise reference, and with what confidence, belongs here.

**Task 2, coexistence.** How do classical identity-bound policies and intent-based policies coexist? Do they compose at one enforcement point, or need separate ones?

**Task 3, runtime verification and conformance verdicts.** Requirements for evaluating an agent's actions against an intent-expressed policy set at the time of action; adjudication when multiple intents are in tension (collision, precedence, criticality); and the conformance verdict the action record (see #1) must be able to carry.

Per discussion on #1, the record should be able to carry a verdict with defined semantics rather than require one, so that deployments with no policy engine in the path remain expressible. That raises two requirements this task carries. First, a carried verdict is a claim by the engine that issued it, so its semantics must cover binding to the issuing engine's identity, freshness, and tamper evidence: a verdict is closer to a small attestation than to a field. Second, absence must be attested rather than merely permitted. If the field is optional and unattested, an operator whose engine returned block is indistinguishable from an operator with no engine in the path, which defeats the verifiability criterion #1 sets. Null semantics are therefore part of verdict semantics.

Per discussion on #5, the policy set is an authored artifact rather
title: [Theme] Intent-based Security Policies: Expression, Coexistence, and Runtime Verification

### What would you like to be added?

This FR requests the implementation of a new SubAgent class: A re-usable component that manages LLM driven tool orchestration. 

This is applicable in the following contexts:
* Allowing a Tool to iteratively solve a problem it encounters. For example, the EditTool using the SubAgent to find a better match string in the case of stale data; or a future "update docstrings" tool, which may call multiple existing tools to find files, edit them and test them.
* Agentic Scopes - Allowing a Tool to be run in an isolated mode - If a tool doesn't manage its' own self healing, and instead expects to do that on the main thread, a SubAgent can be created, which clones the MonoAgent history, executes the tool, and only returns the successful response back to the main thread ()

This FR suggests the most direct path towards implementation would be:
* Create a wrapper around GeminiChat which can drive the GeminiChat::sendMessage*(..) functions either in a nonInteractive, or Interactive function
* Allow a list of filtered tools to be passed to the GeminiChat ContentGenerator::generateContentStream(..) function, so that only a subset of tools may be considered during execution
* Allow a custom system prompt to be provided for GeminiChat to use.
* Allow variable output via a set of private tools that the Agent can use to calculate response data to be accessed via the Caller of the SubAgent.





### Why is this needed?

Currently, GC uses a _mono-agent_ architecture; One SWE Agent which is responsible for all work across the application. While this approach is powerful in its' own right, there's some challenges that it presents:

* Higher Memory Rot - Given that all self healing operations occur in a single History object, there's a higher chance of hallucinations over time as the context history becomes more complex and full of conflicting / stale information. Consider the situation where a file-read occurs, then 2-3 edit attempts that fail, followed by a success. There now may be 5 examples of the same block of code in history memory, which can lead to confusion.
* Lack of SmartTools - The GC Codebase currently has a single agent implementation (GeminiClient + GeminiChat), which means that tools themselves cannot currently support agentic loops in their processing (e.g. recovering from a failure, or orchestrating private tools to execute a task). Further, no other part of the application can engage in Agentic patterns, since there's no primitive to leverage to do so.

### Additional context

Areas of open discussion:
* **Tool permissions** - There's some open discussion that needs to be had about how tool-based permissions work inside subagents. (For example, if you've given ToolX permission to write-always, does that permission also follow forward to when that tool is used inside of a subagent?) 
* **System prompt re-use** - The SubAgent can accept a custom system prompt to drive work, but it may be viable to leverage existing portions of the existing MonoAgent prompt. This is a challenge because the current Mono-Agent system prompt is _powerful_ but also _static_: It currently does not provide a mechanism to be re-used by sub agents, or be broken up in the case of available tools changing. In this case, an ideal solution for SubAgents orchestrating the existing tools may require breaking up prompts.ts to provide a sub-agent the ability to grab examples & multi-shot snippets for a specific tool it is using (which is currently hard-coded into the main prompt).

Important Notes:
* This FR _only_ discusses the addition of the SubAgent primitive, and is not intended to be a solution to larger discussions around mass orchestration of Agents, or their coordinated efforts towards task resolution (e.g. "why not use existing agent-orchestration library X?"). Those are significant architecture conversations that need to happen across the team, as orchestration is a higher level discussion to the SubAgent primitive

## Objective

Replace the current broad global Codex skill/workflow surface with a **minimal issue-to-Draft-PR execution kernel**, while moving build/domain capabilities into project-local `.agents/skills/`.

This is intended as a **one-shot consolidation work unit**, not another incremental taxonomy pass.

Target global kernel:

```text
Franky
Prometheus
Athena

global skills/
├── skill-creator
├── project-agent-setup
├── issue-execution
└── athena-review

+ only genuinely cross-project deterministic utilities that prove reuse
```

Project-local target:

```text
<repo>/
├── AGENTS.md
├── .agents/
│   ├── skills/
│   │   └── project/domain capabilities
│   └── sessions/
│       └── issue-<N>/
│           └── session.yaml
└── project contents
```

The execution loop is:

```text
ChatGPT Cloud
→ stable GitHub Issue
→ Codex reads AGENTS.md + relevant local skills
→ Franky handles agent/runtime/session substrate
→ Prometheus executes bounded work
→ deterministic validation
→ Athena risk-tier independent review
→ bounded repair/re-review
→ Draft PR
→ STOP
→ ChatGPT Cloud audits PR/diff/evidence
→ human merge
```

No automatic merge and no self-acceptance.

---

## Hard rule: clone/adapt skills, do not author from scratch

**Every retained or new global skill in this Issue must be anchored to a maintained upstream skill/spec/example or an already-qualified existing local skill.**

Do **not** start from a blank `SKILL.md` and invent a new procedure merely because the desired behavior is known.

Required sequence:

```text
resolve capability
→ search maintained upstream / installed capability
→ select exact baseline
→ record repository + path + commit/tag/ref + license
→ clone/copy/vendor/symlink as appropriate
→ preserve provenance
→ inspect baseline behavior
→ adapt only what this control plane actually needs
→ run trigger + behavioral + structural evals
→ independent review
→ admit / revise / localize / retire
```

Allowed dispositions:

```text
USE_UPSTREAM_AS_IS
CLONE_AND_ADAPT
REUSE_EXISTING_LOCAL
LOCALIZE_EXISTING
MERGE_EXISTING
RETIRE
DEFER
```

`CREATE_FROM_SCRATCH` is **not a normal disposition**. It is permitted only if no suitable maintained baseline exists and the Issue/PR records the search evidence and explicit justification.

Do not copy content without checking redistribution/license terms.

---

These are required starting points, not optional inspiration.

Primary anchors:

1. OpenAI Codex / Agent Skills system skill creator

2. OpenAI skill evaluation guidance

4. Agent Skills specification/reference material where needed

The implementation must begin by comparing these baselines and selecting the smallest provenance-preserving adaptation strategy.

## B. project-agent-setup

Primary anchors:

1. OpenAI Codex AGENTS.md discovery/precedence guidance  
   - https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md

2. AGENTS.md open format

3. GitHub Awesome Copilot `ai-ready` skill as an external implementation/reference candidate  
   - https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot
   - inspect the current `ai-ready` skill before adaptation

This skill must remain small. It exists to establish project operating instructions, execution profile, protected boundaries, local skill discovery, validation, and issue→Draft-PR behavior. It must not regenerate a documentation architecture.

## C. issue-execution

Use maintained issue-driven/spec-driven execution patterns as anchors before adapting:
